title: R Programming for Agricultural Data Analysis
text:
Preface
Agricultural data describe living systems. A yield measurement reflects a crop, its environment, a management decision, and a method of measurement. R helps us organize those observations and examine the evidence, but it cannot decide whether an experiment was well designed or whether a conclusion makes agricultural sense.
This textbook introduces R through questions that undergraduate students of agriculture can recognize: How variable is yield? Do treatments differ? How does a crop grow? Can weather records help us anticipate future conditions? Students begin with objects and simple calculations, then develop a complete workflow from data entry to a reproducible report.
This book develops my earlier lecture notes for Data Analysis Using Statistical Packages into a detailed undergraduate textbook for the new syllabus. The original explanations, illustrated installation guide, step-by-step R commands, import lessons, descriptive-statistics examples, and time-series walkthrough form the main teaching text. Agricultural applications and additional worked examples extend those lessons. Data cleaning, modern graphics, growth models, inference, field experimental designs, regression, reproducible reporting, and responsible AI-assisted coding complete the seven modules. The aim is to explain what each calculation does, why we use it, and how its result should be interpreted.

title: R Programming for Agricultural Data Analysis
text:
How to study this book
Read an explanation, predict what its code will do, run the code, and compare the output with your prediction. Change one input and explain the result. At the end of each practical, submit both your script and a short interpretation. Code that runs is necessary; a defensible explanation is equally necessary.
The text assumes basic arithmetic, elementary algebra, and introductory statistical concepts. It explains the additional ideas needed for each analysis. No previous programming experience is required. R 4.1 or later is needed for the native pipe |> used throughout.






Real observations and teaching simulations



PlantGrowth, Orange, and iris are datasets distributed with R; their help pages document their origins. The original historical time-series examples are also retained with local data copies and documented sources. The book supplies clearly labelled simulated crop, soil, weather, growth, and pest data for agricultural practice. Simulated results illustrate methods and must never be reported as findings from a field experiment. The data appendix records units, observational units, and limitations.

title: R Programming for Agricultural Data Analysis
text:
A recurring scientific workflow

State a question and identify the observational or experimental unit.
Inspect the design, variable definitions, units, and missing values.
Clean data with a record of every decision.
Summarize and visualize before fitting models.
Select an analysis consistent with the question and design.
Check assumptions and communicate uncertainty and limitations.
Save the code, data provenance, and report so another person can reproduce the work.

This is an editable teaching edition. Instructors should review local terminology, course assessment rules, and the agricultural suitability of examples before adopting it. The earlier project’s licence files are preserved with the source archive; this edition does not assign a new licence.

title: R Programming for Agricultural Data Analysis
text:
Learn by running R






An interactive practical in every chapter



Each teaching chapter now ends with a Live R laboratory: editable code, a Run R button, console output, and plots where appropriate. Start with the first live calculation, or explore growth curves and regression. The browser downloads R on first use. Use a current browser and allow time for the initial download.
Every ordinary code block also has a copy button. Copy commands into RStudio without console prompts or printed results. The full package-based analyses and report rendering are intended for your installed R environment.


The reading layout follows the companion Textbook of Agricultural Statistics: serif explanations, blue headings, gold navigation highlights, and coloured learning boxes. Your original detailed lecture explanations remain the foundation of this edition.

title: Course guide
text:
Suggested practical schedule
R Programming for Agricultural Data Analysis (0+2) introduces programming, data management, graphics, exploratory analysis, growth and time series models, statistical inference, and reproducible communication through practical work.
By completing the course, students should be able to import and validate a dataset; write and modify R scripts; summarize crop, soil, and weather measurements; construct informative figures; randomize and analyse standard field experiments; fit and diagnose introductory models; use AI coding assistants responsibly; and prepare a report that connects evidence to an agricultural question.
The following 18 meetings are a teaching proposal, not an institutional credit-hour rule. Each can be organized as a short demonstration, guided practice, independent work, and discussion. Extend or combine meetings according to the academic calendar.

title: Course guide
text:
Assessment and integrated project
A suggested assessment is 40% practical records, 20% an individual practical test, and 40% an integrated project. Institutions may replace these weights. Assess explanations as well as code.
For the project, select a documented agricultural dataset approved by the instructor. State its source, units, sampling or randomization scheme, and reuse conditions. Ask one primary question. Deliver the raw data or an authorized retrieval script, a cleaning log, a data dictionary, a .qmd report, and a rendered HTML report. Include a table, two complementary figures, an appropriate analysis, diagnostics, and a discussion of limitations. A descriptive project is appropriate when the design does not support inference.
Use this project rubric: question and design (15 marks), data integrity and provenance (20), analysis and diagnostics (25), interpretation and uncertainty (25), reproducibility and presentation (15). A small, carefully justified analysis is preferable to a collection of unrelated tests.

title: Course guide
text:
Classroom workflow
Before class, the instructor runs Rscript scripts/check-environment.R and renders the book. Students open agri-r.Rproj, keep the project folder together, and save work in outputs/. All core datasets are local. Internet access is needed for initial software/package installation and the optional online-import exercise, not for the ordinary chapter examples.
Selected solutions appear in the appendix. Use the other questions for assessment; alternate defensible interpretations are possible. The separate INSTRUCTOR.md gives common misconceptions and teaching advice.

title: 1  Getting started with R
text:
1.1 Learning outcomes
After this chapter, you should be able to explain the roles of R and RStudio in agricultural research, identify the observations and units in an agricultural dataset, create an RStudio project, run and save commands, and install and load a package.

title: 1  Getting started with R
section: 1.2 R and RStudio in agricultural research
text:
1.2 R and RStudio in agricultural research
Agricultural researchers collect observations to answer practical questions: Does a new variety yield more? How do soil nutrient levels vary between fields? What is the response to fertilizer? How does a crop grow through the season? This book teaches you to address such questions using R for analysis and RStudio as your working environment. You will learn to organize observations, inspect their quality, calculate summaries, draw useful graphs, fit appropriate statistical models, and explain the results in agricultural terms.

1.2.1 What R does and what RStudio provides
R is a programming language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. You give it instructions, store observations as objects, and use functions to carry out calculations. An R script records those instructions so you can check an analysis, correct a mistake, or repeat the work with a new dataset. Packages add functions for tasks such as importing Excel files, manipulating data, plotting, and analysing experiments.
RStudio is the interface used for the practicals in this book. Its script editor helps you write and save R commands; its Console runs them; and its supporting panes let you inspect objects, browse files, view plots, and read help. R performs the calculations. RStudio helps you manage the work. Install R first, then RStudio, and keep each research project in its own folder.
Agricultural scientists and students need not become professional software developers. They should, however, understand the commands they use, the observations entering an analysis, and the meaning of its output. Learning R through a research question gives each command a purpose.


1.2.2 Applications across agricultural research
The following examples show how the skills developed in this book contribute to agricultural investigations.








Agricultural question
Observations to organize
Work you will do in R




Do varieties or management treatments differ in yield?
Plot identifiers, treatments, blocks or replicates, and yield with its units
Inspect treatment variation, draw comparative plots, and analyse treatment effects using the experimental design.


How do soil characteristics vary between fields?
Sampling locations, depth, pH, organic carbon, and nutrient measurements
Check missing values and unusual observations, summarize soil properties, and explore relationships.


How does a crop grow during the season?
Plant or plot identifiers, observation dates, and growth measurements
Plot growth trajectories, fit growth models, and interpret their parameters.


How do rainfall and temperature vary over time?
Dates, rainfall, temperature, and measurement units
Visualize time series, examine trends and seasonality, calculate moving averages, and assess forecasts.



Begin by identifying what each row represents. A plot, plant, soil sample, and repeated measurement are different observational units. Preserve treatment and replicate identifiers when importing or cleaning data. Repeated observations on the same plant or plot must not be treated automatically as independent replicates. R can calculate a result even when the data structure or analysis is inappropriate; the researcher must choose a method consistent with the question and design.


1.2.3 From a field notebook to a reproducible analysis
A useful R workflow follows the research process:

Organize: define variables and units, retain the original observations, and import a working copy into R.
Inspect: check data types, missing values, duplicates, and possible entry errors before changing the data.
Explore: use numerical summaries and plots to understand variation and relationships.
Analyse: choose a statistical method suited to the experimental design and check its assumptions.
Communicate: report estimates and uncertainty with an agricultural interpretation, then save the script and exported results.

Software supports statistical reasoning; it does not replace it. Strengthen your understanding of sampling, experimental design, and statistical inference alongside the R practicals. My Textbook of Agricultural Statistics provides a companion reference for the statistical concepts. The chapters that follow develop this workflow through detailed R commands, worked agricultural examples, and practical exercises.
RAISINS is a browser-based platform that offers a graphical route to agricultural data analysis, including statistical summaries and experimental-design analyses. It can complement learning in R by letting students compare a guided analysis with their own R script. Whatever interface is used, students must check the design, assumptions, and interpretation of the results.

title: 1  Getting started with R
section: 1.3 R and RStudio: the illustrated guide
text:
1.3 R and RStudio: the illustrated guide






Using the illustrated installation guide



The download screenshots below were updated on 16 October 2026. The original pane illustration is labelled as historical. Release numbers and screen layouts change; use the official download links given in the text.


This training program is tailored to equip you with the skills needed for agricultural data analysis using R and RStudio. In this introductory section, we will provide you with a brief overview and guide you through the process of installing R and RStudio.

1.3.1 R
R is a programming language for statistical computing and graphics supported by the R Core Team and the R Foundation for Statistical Computing. Created by statisticians Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman. R is an implementation of the S programming language. R is used among data miners, bioinformaticians and statisticians for data analysis and developing statistical software. Users have created packages to augment the functions of the R language. According to user surveys and studies of scholarly literature databases, R is one of the most commonly used programming languages used in data mining. The official R software environment is an open-source free software environment within the GNU package, available under the GNU General Public License. It is written primarily in C, Fortran, and R itself (partially self-hosting). R has a command line interface. Multiple third-party graphical user interfaces are also available, such as RStudio, an integrated development environment.








Figure 1.1: R logo







1.3.2 Rstudio
RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R. It includes a console, syntax-highlighting editor that supports direct code execution, as well as tools for plotting, history, debugging and workspace management. RStudio is available in open source and commercial editions and runs on the desktop (Windows, Mac, and Linux) or in a browser connected to RStudio Server. RStudio is a free and open-source integrated development environment (IDE) for R, a programming language for statistical computing and graphics. JJ Allaire, creator of the programming language ColdFusion, founded RStudio. RStudio is available in two editions: RStudio Desktop, where the program is run locally as a regular desktop application; and RStudio Server, which allows accessing RStudio using a web browser while it is running on a remote Linux server.
The original RStudio interface used the Qt framework; the current desktop application uses Electron. RStudio combines components written in several programming languages. Work on RStudio started at around December 2010, and the first public beta version (v0.92) was officially announced in February 2011.








Figure 1.2: R studio logo





Typical RStudio window has four panes as explained below








Figure 1.3: RStudio pane layout from the original lecture notes; appearance varies in current releases






Console

This is where the action happens. Here any authentic R code typed after the ‘>’ prompt will be executed after pressing ‘Enter’ to generate the output. We will use the Console to run and inspect the commands developed in this book.

Source Editor

This is where R scripts (collection of code) can be created and edited. New R script can be opened by clicking File –> New File –> R Script or using short cut ctrl+shift+N. You can type your codes here. To run a code in console or execute, place the cursor in the line which code is written and press ctrl+enter or highlight the code you wish to evaluate and clicking on the “Run” button on the top right of the Source. You can save your R codes, written in script.

Environment|History|Connections

All of the data objects (such as vectors, matrices, and dataframes) that you have defined in your current R session are listed under the Environment tab of this panel. In data objects, you may also examine details like the quantity of observations and rows. A few other clickable options are available on the tab, such as Import Dataset, which will launch a graphical user interface (GUI) for inputting data into R.
This panel’s History tab only provides a history of all the code that you have previously evaluated in the Console.
The Environment / History panel could be helpful as you become more accustomed to R. However, you can ignore it right now. You can simply just reduce the window by clicking the minimise button in the panel’s upper right corner if you wish to clear up space on your screen.

Files|Plots|Packages|Help|Viewer

You can find a collection of useful information in the Files|Plots|Packages|Help panel. Let’s examine each tab in more detail:
- The file directory on your hard disc is accessible through the files panel. You can utilise the “Files” panel to set your working directory by clicking “More” and then “Set As Working Directory” once you’ve navigated to the folder where you wish to read and save files.

All of your plots are displayed in the Plots panel. There are buttons to export the plot as a pdf or jpg and to open the plot in a separate window.
We are interested in the install button in this pane, to install packages required for our analysis.



1.3.3 Installing the current R release






Installation guide updated 16 October 2026



At the date of this update, CRAN offers R 4.6.1 for Windows and Posit offers RStudio Desktop 2026.10.0, build 233. The screenshots below are genuine captures of the official download pages on that date. Download the stable release displayed when you study this chapter; the version number will change. These are download-page screenshots, rather than screenshots of an installer running on your computer.


Install R first, then RStudio Desktop. R performs the calculations; RStudio provides the editor and working environment.

1.3.3.1 Step 1: choose your operating system
Open CRAN. Choose Download R for Windows on a Windows computer. macOS users should select the macOS download and the installer appropriate to their processor; Linux users should follow CRAN’s instructions for their distribution.



CRAN: choose the download for your operating system. Captured 16 October 2026.




1.3.3.2 Step 2: choose the base installation
On the Windows page, select base or install R for the first time. Rtools is a separate collection of build tools; it is not the R application. Students installing precompiled Windows packages can begin with base R.



CRAN for Windows: choose the base installation. Captured 16 October 2026.




1.3.3.3 Step 3: download and install R
Open the current Windows release page and select its Download R link. At this update it offers R 4.6.1. Check the operating-system requirement on the page: the current R Windows release requires Windows 10 or later and the Universal C Runtime (UCRT).



Current official R for Windows download page, showing R 4.6.1. Captured 16 October 2026.


After downloading, open the installer from your Downloads folder. Select the installation language, read the installation information, and follow Next through the destination and component choices. The defaults are suitable for a typical first installation. Allow installation to finish, then select Finish. Open R from the Start menu to confirm that its console launches. The exact installer screens depend on the release and your system permissions; an institution-managed computer may require laboratory support.



1.3.4 Installing RStudio Desktop

1.3.4.1 Step 4: download the free desktop edition
Open the official RStudio download page. Choose RStudio Desktop, then the installer matching your operating system. The current Windows card lists Windows 11; do not assume RStudio and R have identical operating-system requirements. Select the open-source Desktop installer, rather than the Server or commercial Pro editions, for the course.



Official RStudio Desktop platform choices, release 2026.10.0. Captured 16 October 2026.


Run the downloaded RStudio installer and follow its installation steps. Launch RStudio after completion. RStudio should detect the installed R; if asked to select an R installation, choose the current installation you just installed. On macOS, open the downloaded disk image and follow the application’s installation instructions. Linux users should select the package for their distribution.


1.3.4.2 Step 5: verify the R session
Type the following in RStudio’s Console, without typing the > prompt. These commands report the version actually running on your computer and perform a small calculation.

R.version.string

[1] "R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)"

2 + 3

[1] 5


The version printed in this textbook’s rendered output is the R installation used to build the book; it need not match the latest downloadable release. Your calculation should return 5.
Create a script with File → New File → R Script, enter 2 + 3, and press Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux) or Command+Enter (macOS). Save the script as first-practical.R. If the Source pane is initially absent, opening a script reveals it. The Console, Source, Environment, and Files/Plots/Help areas are described above; modern RStudio also supports an optional Sidebar and customizable pane layouts. See the current official pane guide.






Checkpoint before the first practical



You can open RStudio, run 2 + 3, save an R script, and identify the R version in your Console. Next create a course project and install the packages used in the practicals. Keep an internet connection for the initial package installation.


The original installation pictures are retained with the archived lecture notes in source-notes/ and images/downloadR/; the teaching instructions above use the updated download pages.

title: 1  Getting started with R
text:
1.4 Packages and libraries

1.4.1 Packages
Packages are organised collections of R functions, data, and compiled code. Packages have useful functions to perform specific tasks. Some of the useful packages for agricultural research are agricolae, grapesAgri1 etc.
In the R environment, packages are kept in a directory called “library”. R installs a group of packages by default during installation. Only the default packages are initially available once the R console has been launched. The R application that is getting to use other installed packages needs to be explicitly loaded from package library in order to use them.


1.4.2 Repositories
A repository is where packages are located so that they can be installed from it. Organizations and developers each have their own local repository, which is often online and open to all. The most well-liked R package repositories include: CRAN, BIOCONDUCTOR, GITHUB.

1.4.2.1 CRAN
Comprehensive R Archive Network(CRAN) is the official repository, It is an international network of ftp and web servers run and managed by the R community. It is coordinated by the R community, and before a package can be published in CRAN, it must pass a number of tests to guarantee that it complies with CRAN rules.


1.4.2.2 Bioconductor
Open source software for bioinformatics is designed for the topic-specific repository known as Bioconductor. In keeping with CRAN, it has its own submission and review procedures, and its community is quite active, holding numerous conferences and meetings each year.


1.4.2.3 Github
The most well-known repository for open source projects is Github. Its popularity is due to the unrestricted open source storage space, integration with the version control programme git, and simplicity of sharing and teamwork.



1.4.3 Base packages
Base packages or standard pacakges come pre-installed with R installations and are regarded as being a part of the R source code. The fundamental R functions are found in base packages, which make it possible to perform common statistical and graphical operations on datasets. Examples of Base packages include stats, graphics, grDevices, utils, datasets, methods and base. The functions available in these Base packages can be used for basic operations on the data set. Some of the functions we have discussed earlier in Section Chapter 2, like mean(),min, log10,as.data.frame etc.
The standard installation contains base packages for essential language, statistical, graphics, and utility functions. The exact installed list can be inspected with installed.packages().
In addition, there are fifteen “recommended packages” from CRAN which are included with binary distributions of R: KernSmooth, MASS, Matrix, boot, class, cluster, codetools, foreign, lattice, mgcv, nlme, nnet, rpart, spatial, and survival.


1.4.4 Other packages
Any user could develop a package and make it available through any of the repositories. There are thousands of helpful R packages.


1.4.5 Installing R Packages
There are numerous ways to install R Packages, which are listed below. You need an active internet connectivity for installing packages.

1.4.5.1 From CRAN
Installing Packages From CRAN: For installing Package from CRAN we need the name of the package and use the following command:

install.packages("package name")  

Simply express package name as a character vector in the first argument of the install.packages() function to install more than one package at once:

install.packages(c("grapesAgri1", "MASS"))  



1.4.5.2 From Bioconductor
Bioconductor provides packages for biological data analysis. The original notes used biocLite(). That installation mechanism has been replaced by BiocManager. The distinction between installing its manager and installing a selected package remains useful.

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install(c("GenomicFeatures", "AnnotationDbi"))

Consult the official Bioconductor installation guide for compatibility with your R version. These optional examples are not executed while building the textbook.


1.4.5.3 From github
To install a R package from github, start by installing the devtools package. The best way to do this is from CRAN.

install.packages("devtools")  

Install the package of interest from GitHub using the following code, where you need to remember to list both the author and the name of the package. In this example, we are installing the grapesAgri1 package created by pratheesh3780.

devtools::install_github("pratheesh3780/grapesAgri1")  




1.4.6 Load packages
Once you successfully install an R package; you need to load the package for use in the session. library() function can be used to load package.
Example

library(grapesAgri1)


1.4.6.1 Load Multiple Packages at Once
We need to first specify a vector of package names:

my_packages <- c("dplyr", "mice", "stringr") # vector of package names 
lapply(my_packages, require, character.only = TRUE)    # Load multiple packages  

After running the code, inspect the returned logical values: require() returns FALSE for packages it could not load. Do not assume that every package loaded successfully.



1.4.7 Check, Update and Remove
To check what packages are installed on your computer, type this command:

installed.packages()  

To update all the packages, type this command:

update.packages()  

To update a specific package, type this command:install.packages("package name")

install.packages("grapesAgri1")  



1.4.8 Installation using R studio UI
The packages can be installed using Rstudio User interface. Step by step installation of package grapesAgri1 is shown below. All other packages can be installed in similar way

Step 1: Click on the install button as shown below









Figure 1.4: Step 1






Step 2: Type the name of the package in the window that appears









Figure 1.5: Step 2






Step 3: Select the package name and click install









Figure 1.6: Step 3






Step 4: Load the package name by clicking on the check box.

title: 1  Getting started with R
section: 1.5 Agricultural applications, interpretation, and further practice
text:
1.5 Agricultural applications, interpretation, and further practice

1.5.1 Why use a programming language?
A spreadsheet is convenient for recording observations. A script records the operations performed on them. If a corrected observation arrives, the script can repeat the same analysis. This makes a programming language valuable even for a modest experiment.
R evaluates instructions and stores results as objects. RStudio is an integrated development environment that helps edit scripts, inspect objects, and view plots. R and RStudio are installed separately; both are used in the practicals.
Download R from CRAN and RStudio Desktop from Posit. Follow the installer for your operating system. Open RStudio and create a project in a folder for the course. Keep raw data in data/, scripts in scripts/, and exported results in outputs/. Avoid hard-coded drive names so your work can run on another computer.
The Source pane holds saved scripts; the Console evaluates commands; the Environment pane lists objects; and the Files, Plots, Packages, and Help tabs provide supporting tools. Pane positions may differ. In the Source pane, Ctrl+Enter on Windows runs the selected code or current line. Save your script even when the commands also appear in Console history.


1.5.2 A first agricultural calculation
Suppose a 20-square-metre harvested plot produces 9.6 kg of grain. One hectare contains 10,000 square metres, and one tonne contains 1,000 kg.

grain_kg <- 9.6
plot_area_m2 <- 20
yield_t_ha <- grain_kg / plot_area_m2 * 10000 / 1000
yield_t_ha

[1] 4.8


The answer is 4.8 t/ha. The expression makes the unit conversion explicit. It does not adjust for grain moisture, harvested border rows, or sampling errors; those require additional information. Names such as grain_kg help prevent unit mistakes.
<- assigns a value. A line beginning with # is a comment. R is case sensitive: grain_kg and Grain_kg are different names. The Console’s > prompt is not part of the code. A + prompt usually means that a bracket or quotation mark has not been closed; press Escape and inspect the command.


1.5.3 Packages and help
A package supplies functions, documentation, and sometimes datasets. Install a package once into an R library, then load it in each new session where it is needed. Installation should be a deliberate setup step, not part of rendering an analysis.

install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "readxl"))
library(dplyr)
?mean
example(mean)

The notation dplyr::filter() calls a function explicitly from a package. It is useful when packages provide functions with the same name. For Bioconductor packages, use the current Bioconductor installation instructions and BiocManager; the old biocLite() approach in the earlier notes is obsolete.


1.5.4 Errors are information
“Object not found” suggests a misspelt name, an unrun assignment, or an object from a previous session. “Could not find function” suggests a misspelling or an unloaded package. “Cannot open file” suggests an incorrect relative path. Start with the first error and run a small piece of code that reproduces it. Restart R periodically and run your saved script from the beginning; this reveals hidden dependencies on old objects.


1.5.5 Practical 1 and exercises

Create a course project and save a script containing the yield calculation. Change the harvested mass to 11.2 kg. State the new yield and its unit.
Explain why 9.6 / 20 is not yet a yield in t/ha.
Deliberately type Grain_kg, read the error, and correct it.
Find the help for sqrt() and calculate the square root of 144.

Chapter review. A saved script records an analysis; a project makes file paths portable; packages extend R; and units remain the analyst’s responsibility.

title: 1  Getting started with R
text:
1.6 Live R laboratory

Your first agricultural calculation
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
yield_t_ha <- c(3.2, 3.8, 4.1, 3.5, 4.4)
mean(yield_t_ha)
range(yield_t_ha)
length(yield_t_ha)
Investigate. The five simulated plot yields have a mean of 3.8 t/ha. Change the last yield to 5.4. Predict how the mean and range will change before running again.







From the browser to your practical notebook



Record the input you changed, the output you obtained, and your interpretation. These live examples use base R and work independently. The full chapter examples, including package-based analyses, remain available with copy buttons for RStudio. Browser objects last until this page is reloaded; Reset code restores the editor text. Internet access is needed on first use; long or interactive desktop tasks belong in RStudio.

title: 2  Objects, data structures, and functions
text:
2.1 Learning outcomes
Create and subset vectors, matrices, data frames, and lists; recognize numeric, character, logical, and factor variables; and write a small reusable function.
In this section we will be dealing with basic operations using R. One should be aware of these basics before proceeding to any kind of data analysis using R.
The RStudio interface is simple. You type R code into the bottom line of the RStudio console pane (see figure Figure 1.3) and then click Enter to run it. The code you type is called a command, because it will command your computer to do something for you. The line you type it into is called the command line.
crumbs: 2  Objects, data structures, and functions

title: 2  Objects, data structures, and functions
text:
‘#’ hashtag in R
R treats the hashtag character, ’#’in a special way; R will not run anything that follows a hashtag on a line. This makes hashtags very useful for adding comments and annotations to your code. We will be able to read the comments, but your computer will not process it.
crumbs: 2  Objects, data structures, and functions

title: 2  Objects, data structures, and functions
text:
2.2 Basic arithmetic operations

# Try these codes in R, Type these codes in console and hit enter
# result of R code is also shown here  

# + (Addition)   
7 + 4  

[1] 11

# - (Subtraction)  
7 - 4  

[1] 3

# * (Multiplication)
7 * 2  

[1] 14

# / (division) 
7 / 2  

[1] 3.5

# ^ (exponentiation) 
7 ^ 2

[1] 49


The colon operator (:) returns every integer between two integers. It is an easy way to create a sequence of numbers.

100:130

numeric

2.5.1 Vectors
A combination of multiple values (numeric, character or logical)

How to create a vector
Create a vector: c() for concatenate

2.5.2 Matrices
It’s a homogeneous collection of data sets which is arranged in a two dimensional organisation. It’s a m*n array with similar data type. It is created using a vector input. It has a fixed number of rows and columns. You can perform many arithmetic operations on R matrix like – addition, subtraction, multiplication, and divisions.
Create and naming matrix: matrix(), cbind(), rbind(), rownames(), colnames() Transpose a matrix: t() Dimensions of a matrix: ncol(), nrow(), dim() Get a subset of a matrix: my_data[row, col] Calculations with numeric matrices: rowSums(), colSums(), rowMeans(), colMeans()

# make three vectors c1, c2 and c3

2.5.3 Data frames
A data frame is the data type, we will be going to use frequently. A data frame is like a matrix but can have columns with different types (numeric, character, logical). Rows are observations (individuals) and columns are variables. Function data.frame() is used to create data frame

friends_data <- data.frame(
  name = c("asha", "adhi", "aravind", 
                  "mary"), 
  age = c(20,23,22,21),
  height = c(180, 170, 185, 169),
  married = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)  
)  

# Print
friends_data

     name age height married
1    asha  20    180    TRUE
2    adhi  23    170   FALSE
3 aravind  22    185    TRUE
4    mary  21    169    TRUE


To check whether a data is a data frame, use the is.data.frame() function. Returns TRUE if the data is a data frame:

is.data.frame(friends_data)  

[1] TRUE


To check whether a data is a matrix, data frame or any other class use the function class()

# What is the class of A? --> matrix
class(A)  

[1] "matrix" "array" 

# What is the class of friends_data? --> data.frame
class(friends_data)

[1] "data.frame"


Convert a data class to data frame use the function as.data.frame()

# Convert it as a data frame
A2 <- as.data.frame(A)
# Now, the class is data.frame
class(A2)

[1] "data.frame"


As described in matrix section, you can use the function t() to transpose a data frame:

t(friends_data)

        [,1]   [,2]    [,3]      [,4]  
name    "asha" "adhi"  "aravind" "mary"
age     "20"   "23"    "22"      "21"  
height  "180"  "170"   "185"     "169" 
married "TRUE" "FALSE" "TRUE"    "TRUE"



2.5.3.1 Operations on data frame
Positive indexing by name and by location

# Access the data in 'name' column in friends_data
# dollar sign is used
friends_data$name  

[1] "asha"    "adhi"    "aravind" "mary"   

# or use this
friends_data[, 'name']  

[1] "asha"    "adhi"    "aravind" "mary"   

# Subset columns 1 and 3
friends_data[ , c(1, 3)]  

     name height
1    asha    180
2    adhi    170
3 aravind    185
4    mary    169

# Subset columns 1 to 3  
friends_data[ , c(1:3)]    

     name age height
1    asha  20    180
2    adhi  23    170
3 aravind  22    185
4    mary  21    169


Negative Indexing

# Exclude column 1  

friends_data[, -1]  

  age height married
1  20    180    TRUE
2  23    170   FALSE
3  22    185    TRUE
4  21    169    TRUE


Index by characteristics
We want to select all friends with age greater than or equal to 22.

# Identify rows that meet the condition
friends_data$age >= 22   

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

# TRUE specifies that the row contains a value of age >= 22.


# Select the rows that meet the condition
friends_data[friends_data$age >= 22, ]  

     name age height married
2    adhi  23    170   FALSE
3 aravind  22    185    TRUE

# The R code above, tells R to get all rows from friends_data where age >= 22

If you don’t want to see all the column data for the selected rows but are just interested in displaying, for example, friend names and age for friends with age >= 22, you could use the following R code:

# Use column locations
friends_data[friends_data$age >= 22,  c(1, 2)]  

     name age
2    adhi  23
3 aravind  22

# Or use column names
friends_data[friends_data$age >= 22, c("name", "age")]

     name age
2    adhi  23
3 aravind  22


If you’re finding that your selection statement is starting to be inconvenient, you can put your row and column selections into variables first, such as:

age22 <- friends_data$age >= 22
cols <- c("name", "age")
# Then you can select the rows and columns with those variables:

friends_data[age22, cols]

     name age
2    adhi  23
3 aravind  22


It’s also possible to use the function subset() as follow.

# Select friends data with age >= 22
subset(friends_data, age >= 22)  

     name age height married
2    adhi  23    170   FALSE
3 aravind  22    185    TRUE


Another option is to use the functions attach() and detach(). The function attach() takes a data frame and makes its columns accessible by simply giving their names.

# Attach a data frame
attach(friends_data)
# === Data manipulation ====
friends_data[age>=22, ]

     name age height married
2    adhi  23    170   FALSE
3 aravind  22    185    TRUE

# === End of data manipulation ====
# Detach the data frame
detach(friends_data)

Extend a data frame
Add new column in a data frame

# Add group column to friends_data
data<-c("BSc", "MSc", "Phd", "Btech")
friends_data$degree <- data
friends_data

     name age height married degree
1    asha  20    180    TRUE    BSc
2    adhi  23    170   FALSE    MSc
3 aravind  22    185    TRUE    Phd
4    mary  21    169    TRUE  Btech


It’s also possible to use the functions cbind() and rbind() to extend a data frame.

roll_no<-c(234,235,236,238)
cbind(friends_data, roll_no)

     name age height married degree roll_no
1    asha  20    180    TRUE    BSc     234
2    adhi  23    170   FALSE    MSc     235
3 aravind  22    185    TRUE    Phd     236
4    mary  21    169    TRUE  Btech     238


Calculations with data frame
With numeric data frame, you can use the function rowSums(), colSums(), colMeans(), rowMeans() and apply().

# Following can be used when it is a numeric data frame

# creating a numeric data frame
c1<-c(3,4,5)
c2<-c(7,8,9)
c3<-c(11,12,13)

# Creating matrix by binding column wise  
ex <- cbind(c1,c2,c3)

# converting matrix to data frame
ex<-as.data.frame(ex)
ex

  c1 c2 c3
1  3  7 11
2  4  8 12
3  5  9 13

rowSums(ex)

[1] 21 24 27

colSums(ex)

c1 c2 c3 
12 24 36 

# calculation in non numeric data frame on selected numeric columns
attach(friends_data)
sum(age)

[1] 86

mean(age)

[1] 21.5


apply() function
apply(X, MARGIN, FUN)
Here:
  -x: an array or matrix
-MARGIN:  take a value or range between 1 and 2 to define where to apply the function:
  -MARGIN=1`: the manipulation is performed on rows
-MARGIN=2`: the manipulation is performed on columns
-MARGIN=c(1,2)` the manipulation is performed on rows and columns
-FUN: tells which function to apply. Built functions like mean, median, sum, min, max and even user-defined functions can be applied>


apply(ex,2, mean)

c1 c2 c3 
 4  8 12 

apply(ex,1, mean)

[1] 7 8 9



# Close the final attach() demonstration before continuing.
detach(friends_data)

The attach() examples explain commands encountered in existing scripts. In new analyses, prefer friends_data$age, with(friends_data, mean(age)), or a function with a data = argument. These make the variable source explicit and avoid masking another object with the same name.

text:
2.6 Agricultural applications, interpretation, and further practice

2.6.1 Values and vectors
An atomic vector holds values of one underlying type. Combining numbers and text causes coercion, usually to character. Numeric values support arithmetic; character values describe names; logical values represent TRUE or FALSE. A factor records categories with a specified set of levels.

yield <- c(4.2, 4.8, 5.1, 4.5)
variety <- c("A", "A", "B", "B")
irrigated <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
class(yield)

[1] "numeric"

yield[2]

[1] 4.8

yield[c(1, 3)]

[1] 4.2 5.1

yield[yield > 4.5]

[1] 4.8 5.1

yield * 1000                    # t/ha to kg/ha

[1] 4200 4800 5100 4500

factor(variety, levels = c("A", "B"))

[1] A A B B
Levels: A B


R indexes from 1. Square brackets select elements. > compares values; == tests equality; != tests inequality; and %in% tests membership. Use & and | for elementwise “and” and “or”. Arithmetic is vectorized. R can recycle a shorter vector, so check lengths when combining measurements; recycling does not establish which observations belong together.

plot_id <- 1:4
plot_id[plot_id %in% c(2, 4)]

[1] 2 4

yield[yield >= 4.5 & variety == "B"]

[1] 5.1 4.5

length(yield)

[1] 4




2.6.2 Matrices
A matrix is a rectangular atomic vector with dimensions. It is useful for numeric arrays such as soil measurements at grid positions. A data frame is usually better for a table containing measurements and treatment labels.

soil_grid <- matrix(21:32, nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(soil_grid) <- c("west", "centre", "east")
soil_grid

     west centre east
[1,]   21     22   23
[2,]   24     25   26
[3,]   27     28   29
[4,]   30     31   32

soil_grid[2, 3]

east 
  26 

soil_grid[, "west"]

[1] 21 24 27 30

rowMeans(soil_grid)

[1] 22 25 28 31

colMeans(soil_grid)

  west centre   east 
  25.5   26.5   27.5 

t(soil_grid)

       [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
west     21   24   27   30
centre   22   25   28   31
east     23   26   29   32


x * y multiplies corresponding elements, whereas x %*% y performs matrix multiplication and requires conformable dimensions. Transposing a mixed data frame can coerce its contents to character; select numeric columns before numerical matrix operations.


2.6.3 Data frames and experimental units
A data frame can hold a different type in each column. For a simple field trial, each row should represent one harvested experimental plot, and each column one variable. Treatment labels are ordinary columns and may repeat. Plot identifiers should uniquely identify experimental units; do not use treatment names as unique row names.

field <- data.frame(plot_id, variety = factor(variety), yield_t_ha = yield,
                    irrigated = irrigated)
str(field)

'data.frame':   4 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ plot_id   : int  1 2 3 4
 $ variety   : Factor w/ 2 levels "A","B": 1 1 2 2
 $ yield_t_ha: num  4.2 4.8 5.1 4.5
 $ irrigated : logi  TRUE TRUE FALSE FALSE

field$yield_t_ha

[1] 4.2 4.8 5.1 4.5

field[field$yield_t_ha >= 4.5, c("plot_id", "yield_t_ha")]

  plot_id yield_t_ha
2       2        4.8
3       3        5.1
4       4        4.5

field$yield_kg_ha <- field$yield_t_ha * 1000
summary(field)

    plot_id     variety   yield_t_ha    irrigated        yield_kg_ha  
 Min.   :1.00   A:2     Min.   :4.200   Mode :logical   Min.   :4200  
 1st Qu.:1.75   B:2     1st Qu.:4.425   FALSE:2         1st Qu.:4425  
 Median :2.50           Median :4.650   TRUE :2         Median :4650  
 Mean   :2.50           Mean   :4.650                   Mean   :4650  
 3rd Qu.:3.25           3rd Qu.:4.875                   3rd Qu.:4875  
 Max.   :4.00           Max.   :5.100                   Max.   :5100  


field[rows, columns] separates row and column selection by a comma. A blank position means all rows or all columns. Prefer explicit names and data = arguments over attach(), which can obscure where a variable comes from.


2.6.4 Lists, missing values, and functions
A list can contain objects of different structures. Statistical model results are often lists. $ or [[ ]] extracts a component, while [ ] keeps a sublist.

trial <- list(site = "Teaching farm", observations = field,
              units = "t/ha")
trial$site

[1] "Teaching farm"

trial[["observations"]]

  plot_id variety yield_t_ha irrigated yield_kg_ha
1       1       A        4.2      TRUE        4200
2       2       A        4.8      TRUE        4800
3       3       B        5.1     FALSE        5100
4       4       B        4.5     FALSE        4500

x <- c(4.2, NA, 5.1)
is.na(x)

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

mean(x)

[1] NA

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 4.65


NA records an unknown value. It is neither zero nor the character string "NA". Use is.na(x), not x == NA. NaN is an undefined numeric result and Inf represents infinity. Removing missing values from a calculation changes its denominator and may change the population represented by the result.
A function names a repeatable calculation. Arguments supply inputs and the final expression supplies the return value.

to_t_ha <- function(mass_kg, area_m2) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(mass_kg), all(is.finite(mass_kg)),
            all(mass_kg >= 0), is.numeric(area_m2),
            length(area_m2) == 1, is.finite(area_m2), area_m2 > 0)
  mass_kg / area_m2 * 10
}
to_t_ha(c(9.6, 11.2), 20)

[1] 4.8 5.6


The checks stop the calculation for invalid inputs. Later, the pipe |> passes a result into the first argument of the next function: sqrt(16) and 16 |> sqrt() are equivalent. A pipe expresses a sequence, not a new statistical method.


2.6.5 Practical 2 and exercises

Create a vector from 1 to 30. Select values below 8, then values below 8 or above 12, and finally 2, 6, and 12. This extends the earlier self-assessment exercises.
Create a four-row, five-column matrix from 1 to 20. Calculate its row means and select row 2, column 3.
Construct a six-plot data frame with a unique identifier, variety, and yield. Select yields above the overall mean.
Store the data frame and a description in a list. Explain why an atomic vector is unsuitable for this task.
Predict the type of c(1, "2"); verify it. Why could this matter when importing data?

Chapter review. Choose structures according to the information they represent. An identifier, a category, and a measurement may all look like numbers but play different analytical roles.

2.7 Original self-assessment exercises
The following exercises retain the tasks from the author’s original self-assessment document. Attempt them before looking at a solution. For each task, save the command, its output, and a short explanation. The later chapters return to the import and statistical-summary tasks with more detail.

Calculate the sum of two numbers. Create variables num1 and num2, assign them two numbers, and then calculate their sum.
Convert temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit. Create temp_celsius, assign a temperature in Celsius, and calculate Fahrenheit using (temp_celsius * 9/5) + 32. State the units of the input and output.
Calculate the area of a rectangle. Create variables for length and width, assign the dimensions, and calculate their product. If dimensions are in metres, state the unit of the area. Prefer plot_length and plot_width to names that shadow common functions.
Calculate the factorial of a number. Assign a nonnegative integer to num and calculate its factorial using a built-in function. Explain the meaning of the answer for a small integer.
Determine whether a number is even or odd. Assign an integer to num, use the remainder operator %%, and print an appropriate result. What does num %% 2 == 0 test?
Calculate a square root. Assign a nonnegative number to num and calculate its square root using a built-in function. Explain why a negative input requires a different numerical interpretation.
Generate a sequence of numbers. Create a sequence from 1 to 10 using a built-in function; compare it with 1:10.
Create a vector and calculate its length. Use elements of your choice, inspect the vector’s class, and calculate its length.
Filter elements in a vector. Create a numeric vector and remove elements greater than a chosen threshold using logical indexing. State whether your condition selects values to keep or values to discard.
Create a CSV file of the iris dataset. Load iris, export it with row.names = FALSE, and identify where the file was saved.
Perform basic statistical calculations on iris. Import the CSV, calculate the mean, median, and standard deviation for each numeric measurement column, and summarize species as a category. Explain why it is inappropriate to average the species names.

For a further agricultural application, write a function that converts a vector of harvested grain masses to t/ha using a common harvested area. Check that the area is positive and demonstrate the function on at least three observations. This connects the original programming exercises with the yield calculation in the opening chapter.

title: 3  Importing, validating, and exporting data
text:
3.1 Learning outcomes
Prepare a rectangular data file, import CSV and Excel files, retrieve a documented online file, validate imported values, and export data without accidental row-number columns.
In the previous chapter we have discussed the very basics of R programming including installation, launching, basic data types and arithmetic functions. Here, you will learn how to import data into R. It is important to ensure that your data is well prepared before importing it into R to avoid errors.
crumbs: 3  Importing, validating, and exporting data

title: 3  Importing, validating, and exporting data
text:
3.2 Preparing your file

File can be prepared in MS Excel
Use the first row as column headers (or column names). Generally, columns represent variables.
Keep a unique observation identifier in an ordinary column. Generally rows represent observations; an identifier need not be assigned as R row names.
Make each observation identifier unique. In experiments, treatment labels should repeat across replicates in a separate treatment column; treatment names are not unique plot identifiers.

Column names should be compatible with R naming conventions.

3.2.1 Naming conventions:

Avoid names with blank spaces. Bad column name Sepal width; Good convention Sepal_width
Avoid names with special symbols: ?, $, *, +, #, (, ), -, /, }, {, |, >, < etc. Letters, digits, underscores, and dots can be used in ordinary syntactic names; a simple naming convention is easier to maintain.
Avoid beginning variable names with a number. Use letter instead. Good column names: obs_100m or x100m. Bad column name: 100m
Column names must be unique. Duplicated names are not allowed.
R is case sensitive. This means that Name, NAME and name, naMe all are treated as different.
Avoid blank rows in your data
Delete any comments in your file
Replace missing values by NA (denotes Not Available)
If you have a column containing date, use the four digit format. Good format: 01/01/2016. Bad format: 01/01/16

A final good looking file








Figure 3.1: An example file







3.2.2 Saving file
I recommend you to save your file in .csv (comma separated value file) format.
Why CSV?
The usual file we save in MS Excel will be saved as XLS files or XLSX files. Workbook files for Microsoft Excel from 97 to 2003 are known as XLS files. The XLSX extension is used by later versions of Excel. All of the data from the worksheets in a workbook, including formatting, charts, graphics, calculations, and more, is contained in the XLS and XLSX file formats.
The Comma Separated Values (CSV) format is a plain text format in which values are separated by commas, whereas the Excel Sheets binary file format (XLS) contains information on all of the worksheets in a file, including both content and formatting. Any spreadsheet programme, including Microsoft Excel, Open Office, Google Sheets, etc., can open CSV files. A straightforward text editor can also be used to open CSV files. Because it is straightforward and compatible with the majority of platforms, it is a very prevalent and well-liked file format for storing and accessing data. But there are certain drawbacks to this simplicity. CSV files can only contain a single sheet without any formatting or formulas.
While CSV files are supported by almost all data upload interfaces, Excel (XLS and XLSX) file types are preferable for storing more complicated data. The CSV file format may be more advantageous if you intend to move your data between platforms or export and import it between interfaces.


3.2.3 How to save as csv
Under the "File name" section in the "Save As" tab, you can select "Save as type" and change it to "CSV (Comma delimited) (*.csv).

3.11 Agricultural applications, interpretation, and further practice

3.11.1 Prepare the table before analysis
Use one header row, one observational unit per row, and one variable per column. Record units in a data dictionary. Avoid merged cells, colour-coded values without a corresponding variable, and subtotals mixed into observations. Keep raw files unchanged. Store corrections in code and separate outputs. Use explicit identifiers rather than relying on row order.
Names such as yield_t_ha and ISO dates such as 2024-06-15 reduce ambiguity. R can handle nonstandard column names with backticks, but simple unique names are easier to teach and maintain. CSV stores values in a single plain-text table; it does not preserve spreadsheet formatting, formulas, or multiple worksheets.


3.11.2 Import and inspect a CSV

readxl reads Excel workbooks without requiring Java. The supplied workbook contains a trial sheet with the same simulated observations as the CSV.

Use CSV for broad interchange and RDS when R-specific classes must be preserved. Excel supports multiple sheets. CSV may lose factor levels and other metadata. Always reopen an export and inspect it.


3.11.4 Online sources and provenance
Online agricultural databases may offer downloadable CSV files or an API. Consult the provider’s documentation, select the crop, location, unit, time period, and aggregation level, and save the query and retrieval date. A district’s annual yield is not an individual farmer’s yield. Do not mix administrative totals with plot-level measurements.
The following optional example retrieves a botanical dataset from the Rdatasets mirror of R datasets. The authoritative dataset description remains R’s ?iris documentation. It teaches a download workflow; a production agricultural database will have its own schema and access rules. It is excluded from routine rendering because it requires network access.

url <- "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/datasets/iris.csv"
download.file(url, "data/iris_online.csv", mode = "wb")
online <- read.csv("data/iris_online.csv")
str(online)
writeLines(c(paste("Source:", url), paste("Retrieved:", Sys.Date())),
           "data/iris_online_provenance.txt")

Check the downloaded schema before analysis; providers can revise URLs and file formats. For the main lessons, use the bundled local datasets. The data appendix links to official R dataset documentation and describes the generated examples.


3.11.5 Practical 3 and exercises

Import the CSV and Excel files. Compare dimensions, column names, and the first six yields.
Export only plot_id, treatment, and yield_t_ha; reopen the file and confirm that no extra row-number column appeared.
Explain why a blank yield cannot safely be changed to zero.
With instructor guidance, locate an official crop-production table. Record its source, time coverage, unit, geographical level, and reuse conditions before importing it. Explain whether its rows are independent experimental units.

Chapter review. Successful data exchange includes a check of meaning, units, and structure, not just a successful read command.

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
text:
4.1 Learning outcomes
Identify missingness, duplicated records, inconsistent categories, and unusual observations; repair column types, labels, dates, and units; apply validation rules; distinguish a correction from an analytical choice; and document cleaning decisions in a reproducible script.

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
text:
4.2 Why a cleaning log matters
A field sheet may contain a repeated entry, a missed harvest, or a measurement in the wrong unit. These are different problems. A duplicate entry may be removed after checking its identity; a missing harvest remains unknown; and a unit error requires evidence before correction. A cleaning log records the identifier, issue, action, reason, and source of verification.
The supplied crop_dirty.csv is a teaching copy with deliberate problems. It contains 61 rows for 60 unique plots, an inconsistent treatment label, two missing yields, and one suspiciously high yield. The clean file is a separate simulation, not evidence that students could ordinarily reconstruct unknown measurements.

dirty <- read.csv("data/crop_dirty.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
colSums(is.na(dirty))

       plot_id          block      treatment        variety      replicate 
             0              0              0              0              0 
nitrogen_kg_ha    rainfall_mm     yield_t_ha 
             0              0              2 

dirty[duplicated(dirty$plot_id) |
        duplicated(dirty$plot_id, fromLast = TRUE), ]

   plot_id block treatment variety replicate nitrogen_kg_ha rainfall_mm
5     P005     1   Compost       A         1           63.1       581.8
61    P005     1   Compost       A         1           63.1       581.8
   yield_t_ha
5        3.52
61       3.52

table(dirty$treatment, useNA = "ifany")


 control    Compost   Control   Mineral 
        1        21        19        20 


An exact duplicate repeats every field. A repeated identifier with different measurements needs investigation, not automatic deletion. In this exercise the extra row is an exact duplicate, so removing it is defensible.

clean <- unique(dirty)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(clean$plot_id))
clean$treatment <- trimws(clean$treatment)
clean$treatment[clean$treatment == "control"] <- "Control"
stopifnot(all(clean$treatment %in% c("Control", "Compost", "Mineral")))

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
text:
4.3 Missing data and denominators
Missingness can be informative: flood-damaged plots may be harder to harvest, and the same flooding can reduce yield. Omitting them could bias a treatment comparison. na.rm = TRUE excludes missing measurements from a calculation; it does not repair the experiment. Report how many measurements were available and investigate why values are missing.

data.frame(n_total = nrow(clean),
           n_observed = sum(!is.na(clean$yield_t_ha)),
           n_missing = sum(is.na(clean$yield_t_ha)),
           mean_observed = mean(clean$yield_t_ha, na.rm = TRUE))

  n_total n_observed n_missing mean_observed
1      60         58         2      4.386034


Do not replace all missing observations with the mean. This reduces apparent variation and understates uncertainty. Methods such as multiple imputation require explicit assumptions and are beyond this introductory course.

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
section: 4.4 Flag outliers; do not delete them automatically
text:
4.4 Flag outliers; do not delete them automatically
An outlier is unusual relative to a distribution or model. A large yield may be a data-entry error, an unusually productive plot, or evidence that groups should be analyzed separately. The interquartile range (IQR) rule flags observations outside Q1 - 1.5 IQR and Q3 + 1.5 IQR; it does not establish that they are wrong.

q <- quantile(clean$yield_t_ha, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)
spread <- diff(q)
clean$flag_yield <- !is.na(clean$yield_t_ha) &
  (clean$yield_t_ha < q[1] - 1.5 * spread |
   clean$yield_t_ha > q[2] + 1.5 * spread)
clean[clean$flag_yield, c("plot_id", "yield_t_ha")]

   plot_id yield_t_ha
10    P010       40.5


For this exercise only, the provided correction ledger represents a checked field sheet. It confirms that plot P010 was entered with a decimal error. Missing yields remain missing. In real work, keep the actual supporting document and record who checked it.

ledger <- read.csv("data/corrections.csv")
clean$yield_t_ha[match(ledger$plot_id, clean$plot_id)] <- ledger$correct_yield_t_ha
clean$flag_yield <- NULL
audit <- data.frame(
  issue = c("Exact duplicate", "Treatment spelling", "P010 decimal error", "Missing yields"),
  action = c("Removed repeated row", "Standardized to Control",
             "Used supplied verified ledger", "Retained as NA"))
audit

               issue                        action
1    Exact duplicate          Removed repeated row
2 Treatment spelling       Standardized to Control
3 P010 decimal error Used supplied verified ledger
4     Missing yields                Retained as NA

dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(clean, "outputs/crop_cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(audit, "outputs/cleaning_log.csv", row.names = FALSE)

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
section: 4.5 Distinguishing missing, zero, and below-detection observations
text:
4.5 Distinguishing missing, zero, and below-detection observations
Let us consider three entries in a soil analysis sheet: 0, an empty cell, and <2. These entries do not mean the same thing. Zero claims that the measured quantity is zero on the stated scale. An empty cell usually says that the measurement is unavailable. <2 says that the laboratory could not quantify the concentration below a reporting limit of 2 in the stated unit. If all three are converted to zero, information about the measurement process is lost.
Before converting a character column to numeric, inspect the distinct entries. Suppose a technician used -999 for a missing reading. That number may be numerically valid to R even though it is not a possible crop yield. The program cannot infer the field-sheet convention on its own.

recorded <- c("4.8", "", "-999", "5.2", "NA")
missing_codes <- c("", "-999", "NA")
recorded[recorded %in% missing_codes] <- NA_character_
validated_yield <- as.numeric(recorded)
validated_yield

[1] 4.8  NA  NA 5.2  NA


Here the missing-code list comes from the example’s recording protocol. Do not assume that a negative value is always missing; negative temperature or a negative change in biomass can be meaningful. A below-detection entry needs a separate indicator or a method appropriate to censored measurements. Substituting half the detection limit by habit can distort a distribution, especially when many values are below the limit.
The same principle applies to dates and units. A date such as 03/04/2024 could mean 3 April or 4 March. A number recorded in kilograms cannot be combined with tonnes merely because the column has a numeric type. Resolve these ambiguities using the source and document the resolution before fitting a model.

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
text:
4.6 Checking the design while cleaning
Data quality includes the arrangement of observations. In a trial with three treatments in each of six blocks, a missing treatment-by-block combination may signal a lost plot or an import error. A missing response and a missing entire row are different: is.na() detects the former but cannot detect a plot that is absent from the table.

rcbd <- read.csv("data/rcbd.csv")
expected_design <- expand.grid(block = 1:6,
                              treatment = c("Control", "Compost", "Mineral"),
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
missing_plots <- dplyr::anti_join(expected_design, rcbd,
                                  by = c("block", "treatment"))
missing_plots

[1] block     treatment
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

with(rcbd, table(block, treatment))

     treatment
block Compost Control Mineral
    1       1       1       1
    2       1       1       1
    3       1       1       1
    4       1       1       1
    5       1       1       1
    6       1       1       1


The empty result from anti_join() means every expected combination is represented. It does not prove that the treatments were randomized correctly or that identifiers were transcribed correctly. Those questions require the field layout and randomization record. Cleaning and experimental design therefore meet at the point where a row is interpreted as an experimental unit.

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
section: 4.7 A sensitivity analysis for a doubtful observation
text:
4.7 A sensitivity analysis for a doubtful observation
Sometimes a value remains doubtful after checking the source. It may be reasonable to report analyses with and without that observation, while identifying the choice as a sensitivity analysis. The aim is to discover how strongly a conclusion depends on one record, not to select whichever analysis gives the desired answer.

trial <- read.csv("data/crop_trial.csv")
high_id <- trial$plot_id[which.max(trial$yield_t_ha)]
mean_all <- mean(trial$yield_t_ha)
mean_without_highest <- mean(trial$yield_t_ha[trial$plot_id != high_id])
data.frame(analysis = c("All observations", "Highest observation omitted"),
           n = c(nrow(trial), nrow(trial) - 1),
           mean_yield_t_ha = c(mean_all, mean_without_highest))

                     analysis  n mean_yield_t_ha
1            All observations 60        3.772000
2 Highest observation omitted 59        3.748475


This calculation does not justify removing the highest plot. It makes the effect of an exclusion visible. For treatment inference, repeat the appropriate design-based model rather than comparing overall means alone. If the conclusion changes substantially, discuss that instability and the reason for the disputed observation.

title: 4  Cleaning agricultural observations
section: 4.8 Cleaning a messy field book step by step
text:
4.8 Cleaning a messy field book step by step
Real field books are typed by people working quickly, often from handwritten sheets. The simulated file field_book_messy.csv contains twelve plots from a variety trial with a net harvested area of 5 m² per plot. It has the problems you will meet most often: inconsistent labels, a comma used as a decimal mark, several codes for “not recorded”, dates in day/month/year order, a value entered in the wrong unit, and a probable decimal slip.

4.8.1 Step 1: import with the missing-value codes you know about
Start by reading the file as it is and inspecting the structure. Tell read.csv() which entries mean “missing” in this field book.

fb <- read.csv("data/field_book_messy.csv",
               na.strings = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-"))
str(fb)

'data.frame':   12 obs. of  7 variables:
 $ plot           : chr  "P01" "P02" "P03" "P04" ...
 $ sowing_date    : chr  "05/06/2025" "05/06/2025" "06/06/2025" "06/06/2025" ...
 $ variety        : chr  "V1" "v1 " "V2" "V2" ...
 $ plant_height_cm: chr  "84.5" "86.1" "79,8" "81.0" ...
 $ tillers        : int  12 14 11 NA 15 13 12 10 16 13 ...
 $ grain_wt_g_plot: num  2410 2550 2190 2275 2620 ...
 $ remarks        : chr  NA NA NA "tillers not counted" ...


str() shows the first problem. plant_height_cm was read as character, not numeric, because one entry contains a comma. Any column that should be numeric but appears as chr needs investigation before analysis. tillers and grain_wt_g_plot were read as numbers because - and n/a were declared as missing.


4.8.2 Step 2: repair types without losing information
Look at the offending entries before converting them. Converting directly with as.numeric() would silently turn "79,8" into NA.

fb$plant_height_cm[is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(fb$plant_height_cm)))]

[1] "79,8" NA    

fb$plant_height_cm <- as.numeric(gsub(",", ".", fb$plant_height_cm))
summary(fb$plant_height_cm)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
  78.90   80.70   85.20  154.59   91.15  850.00       1 


gsub(",", ".", x) replaces every comma with a decimal point. The only remaining missing height is the lodged plot recorded as n/a, which is a genuine missing value with a reason in the remarks column. The summary also exposes a maximum height of 850 cm, which we return to in step 5.


4.8.3 Step 3: standardize category labels

table(fb$variety, useNA = "ifany")


 V3  V1 v1   V2  v3  V3 
  1   3   1   4   1   2 

fb$variety <- toupper(trimws(fb$variety))
table(fb$variety)


V1 V2 V3 
 4  4  4 

stopifnot(all(fb$variety %in% c("V1", "V2", "V3")))

trimws() removes leading and trailing spaces and toupper() converts to capitals. Before the fix, R counted six different variety labels; afterwards, three varieties with four plots each. The stopifnot() line will stop the script if a new unexpected label ever appears.


4.8.4 Step 4: convert dates explicitly
Dates typed as 05/06/2025 are ambiguous: 5 June or 6 May? The field protocol states day/month/year, so we give that format to as.Date().

fb$sowing_date <- as.Date(fb$sowing_date, format = "%d/%m/%Y")
range(fb$sowing_date)

[1] "2025-06-05" "2025-06-10"

stopifnot(!anyNA(fb$sowing_date))
harvest <- as.Date("2025-10-01")
fb$days_to_harvest <- as.numeric(harvest - fb$sowing_date)
head(fb[, c("plot", "sowing_date", "days_to_harvest")], 3)

  plot sowing_date days_to_harvest
1  P01  2025-06-05             118
2  P02  2025-06-05             118
3  P03  2025-06-06             117


In the format string, %d is day, %m is month number, and %Y is the four-digit year. If any date fails to match the format, as.Date() returns NA, which the stopifnot() check catches. Once a column has the Date class, subtraction gives the number of days between dates.


4.8.5 Step 5: check values against plausible ranges
A validation rule states the range of plausible values for each variable. The limits come from agronomic knowledge, not from the data themselves. A value outside the range is flagged for checking, not changed.

rules <- data.frame(variable = c("plant_height_cm", "tillers", "grain_wt_g_plot"),
                    min = c(30, 1, 500),
                    max = c(150, 40, 5000))
flags <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(rules)), function(i) {
  v <- rules$variable[i]
  x <- fb[[v]]
  bad <- which(!is.na(x) & (x < rules$min[i] | x > rules$max[i]))
  if (length(bad)) data.frame(plot = fb$plot[bad], variable = v, value = x[bad])
}))
flags

  plot        variable  value
1  P10 plant_height_cm 850.00
2  P07 grain_wt_g_plot   2.43


Two plots are flagged. P07 has a grain weight of 2.43, which is impossible for a 5 m² plot in grams but plausible in kilograms; the remarks column says it was weighed in kilograms. P10 has a height of 850 cm, ten times the heights of the other plots of V1, which suggests a missing decimal point.


4.8.6 Step 6: apply only documented corrections
For this exercise, assume the original field sheets were checked: P07 was confirmed as 2.43 kg, and P10 as 85.0 cm. Record the corrections in a table and apply them from that table, so the log and the data cannot drift apart.

fixes <- data.frame(
  plot = c("P07", "P10"),
  variable = c("grain_wt_g_plot", "plant_height_cm"),
  old_value = c(2.43, 850),
  new_value = c(2430, 85.0),
  reason = c("Weighed in kg; converted to g (field sheet checked)",
             "Decimal point omitted (field sheet checked)"))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(fixes))) {
  row <- fb$plot == fixes$plot[i]
  stopifnot(sum(row) == 1, fb[row, fixes$variable[i]] == fixes$old_value[i])
  fb[row, fixes$variable[i]] <- fixes$new_value[i]
}
fixes

  plot        variable old_value new_value
1  P07 grain_wt_g_plot      2.43      2430
2  P10 plant_height_cm    850.00        85
                                               reason
1 Weighed in kg; converted to g (field sheet checked)
2         Decimal point omitted (field sheet checked)


The stopifnot() inside the loop confirms that each plot exists exactly once and still holds the old value before it is changed. If someone has already corrected the file, the script stops instead of applying a correction twice.


4.8.7 Step 7: convert units and save
Grain weight in grams per 5 m² plot converts to tonnes per hectare by dividing by the plot area (g/m²), multiplying by 10,000 m²/ha, and dividing by 1,000,000 g/t.

net_plot_m2 <- 5
fb$yield_t_ha <- fb$grain_wt_g_plot / net_plot_m2 * 10000 / 1e6
round(tapply(fb$yield_t_ha, fb$variety, mean), 2)

  V1   V2   V3 
4.89 4.41 5.23 

dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(fb, "outputs/field_book_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(fixes, "outputs/field_book_corrections.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The raw file in data/ is never overwritten. Anyone can rerun the script from the raw file and obtain the same clean file and the same correction log.






A cleaning checklist




Keep the raw file unchanged; clean with a script.
Declare missing-value codes at import and check str().
Inspect entries that fail numeric conversion before converting.
Standardize labels and check them against the list of valid levels.
Convert dates with an explicit format and confirm none became NA.
Check every numeric variable against agronomically plausible ranges.
Correct only with evidence, from a corrections table, and keep the log.
Confirm units and convert them explicitly.
Check the design: every expected plot present, no duplicates.
Save the clean data and the log separately from the raw data.

text:
4.10 Live R laboratory

Keep an explicit cleaning record
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
soil <- data.frame(plot = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 4),
                   pH = c(5.8, 6.2, 6.2, NA, 65))
soil$duplicate <- duplicated(soil[c("plot", "pH")])
soil$needs_check <- is.na(soil$pH) | soil$pH < 0 | soil$pH > 14
soil
clean <- subset(soil, !duplicate & !needs_check)
mean(clean$pH)
Investigate. The value 65 needs verification against the field record. Flagging it does not establish its correct replacement. Explain which rows were excluded from this temporary summary.
