cv(a) = 11.5 %, cv(b) = 3 %, Mean = 4.731111 


Comparisons in a split-plot need care, because different comparisons use different errors. Two main-plot means use error (a); two subplot means at the same main-plot level use error (b); two subplot means at different main-plot levels combine both errors. Standard textbooks such as Gomez and Gomez (1984) give these formulas. In practice, state which comparison you are making and which error it uses.

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.10 Checking assumptions and transforming data
The F-test assumes that errors are independent, have constant variance, and are approximately normal. Independence comes from randomization. Constant variance and normality are checked with the residuals of the fitted model, as in the previous chapter.

old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(rb_fit, which = 1)
plot(rb_fit, which = 2)







par(old)

Agricultural data often break the constant-variance assumption in a predictable way. Counts, such as insects per plant or weeds per quadrat, have variance that increases with the mean. Percentages based on counts, such as germination or disease incidence, have small variance near 0% and 100% and large variance near 50%. For such data a transformation can stabilize the variance before analysis.

13.10.1 Counts: square-root transformation
The simulated file aphid_counts.csv records aphids per plant under five treatments in a CRD with five plants each.

ap <- read.csv("data/aphid_counts.csv")
ap$treatment <- factor(ap$treatment)
# Mean and variance by treatment: variance rises with the mean
round(t(sapply(split(ap$aphids_per_plant, ap$treatment),
               function(x) c(mean = mean(x), variance = var(x)))), 1)

              mean variance
Control       41.2    246.7
Insecticide A  5.6     15.3
Insecticide B  8.6     21.3
Insecticide C  3.8      1.2
Neem oil      20.0     53.5

bartlett.test(aphids_per_plant ~ treatment, data = ap)


    Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances

data:  aphids_per_plant by treatment
Bartlett's K-squared = 20.405, df = 4, p-value = 0.0004154

ap$sqrt_count <- sqrt(ap$aphids_per_plant + 0.5)
bartlett.test(sqrt_count ~ treatment, data = ap)


    Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances

data:  sqrt_count by treatment
Bartlett's K-squared = 7.5716, df = 4, p-value = 0.1086

ap_fit <- aov(sqrt_count ~ treatment, data = ap)
summary(ap_fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)    
treatment    4  64.00  16.001   20.46 7.7e-07 ***
Residuals   20  15.64   0.782                    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The control has a much larger variance than the effective insecticides. Bartlett’s test is clearly significant for the raw counts; after the transformation, much less heterogeneity remains. Adding 0.5 before taking the square root is recommended when counts include zeros or small values.
Carry out comparisons on the transformed scale and report means on both scales. Transformed means can be converted back for presentation; the back-transformed value of a mean square root is not the arithmetic mean count, so label it clearly.

sqrt_means <- tapply(ap$sqrt_count, ap$treatment, mean)
data.frame(mean_count = round(tapply(ap$aphids_per_plant, ap$treatment, mean), 1),
           mean_sqrt = round(sqrt_means, 2),
           back_transformed = round(sqrt_means^2 - 0.5, 1))

              mean_count mean_sqrt back_transformed
Control             41.2      6.35             39.8
Insecticide A        5.6      2.31              4.8
Insecticide B        8.6      2.94              8.1
Insecticide C        3.8      2.06              3.7
Neem oil            20.0      4.48             19.6

design_stats(ap_fit, r = 5)

       MSE        SEm        SEd         CD CV_percent 
     0.782      0.395      0.559      1.167     24.381 


The CD applies to the mean_sqrt column, not to the counts.


13.10.2 Percentages: angular (arcsine) transformation
For percentages from counts, the angular transformation \(\sin^{-1}\sqrt{p}\) stabilizes the variance, where \(p\) is the proportion. It is most useful when many values lie below 30% or above 70%.

ge <- read.csv("data/germination.csv")
ge$seed_treatment <- factor(ge$seed_treatment)
ge$angle_deg <- asin(sqrt(ge$germination_pct / 100)) * 180 / pi
ge_fit <- aov(angle_deg ~ seed_treatment, data = ge)
summary(ge_fit)

               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
seed_treatment  3 1448.1   482.7   40.88 1.41e-06 ***
Residuals      12  141.7    11.8                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

angle_means <- tapply(ge$angle_deg, ge$seed_treatment, mean)
data.frame(mean_pct = tapply(ge$germination_pct, ge$seed_treatment, mean),
           mean_angle = round(angle_means, 2),
           back_transformed_pct = round(100 * sin(angle_means * pi / 180)^2, 1))

          mean_pct mean_angle back_transformed_pct
GA3           92.5      74.40                 92.8
Hot water     72.5      58.42                 72.6
KNO3          84.0      66.53                 84.1
Untreated     56.5      48.77                 56.6


asin() returns radians; multiplying by 180 / pi gives degrees, the scale used in most agricultural tables.






Transformations and modern alternatives



Transformations are the classical remedy and remain common in Indian agricultural research reports. Generalized linear models, such as Poisson models for counts and binomial models for germination, analyse the data on their original scale. They are beyond this introductory course but worth knowing about when you meet them in journals. A transformation should be chosen because of the type of data, not because it makes a result significant.

13.11 Comparing treatment means
A significant F-test says that at least one treatment mean differs. Researchers then want to know which ones. Several procedures are in common use, and they answer slightly different questions.

Procedure
What it controls
When it is suitable




CD / LSD
Error rate of each comparison
Planned comparisons, or a few comparisons after a significant F-test (Fisher’s protected LSD)


Duncan’s multiple range test (DMRT)
Error rate that depends on how far apart means are in the ranking
Traditionally used to rank many varieties; widely seen in Indian journals


Tukey’s HSD
Error rate for the whole family of pairwise comparisons

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.12 Missing plots and other designs
Plots are sometimes lost to flooding, animals, or theft. In a balanced design, a missing plot makes the data unbalanced. Classical textbooks give formulas to estimate a single missing value in an RCBD or Latin square. Software that fits the model by least squares, including lm(), can analyse unbalanced data directly, but with unbalanced data the order of terms in aov() matters, and the interpretation needs more care. Record why each plot is missing; if losses depend on the treatment, they are themselves a result.
Other designs are used in agricultural research for special situations: augmented designs for screening many germplasm lines with limited seed, lattice and alpha designs for large variety trials where complete blocks would be too big, and strip-plot designs where two factors are both applied to strips. They follow the same principles but need a dedicated text, such as Gomez and Gomez’s Statistical Procedures for Agricultural Research.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.13 Reporting a field experiment
A complete report of a designed experiment states:

The design, number of treatments, replications, and plot size, and how randomization was done.
The experimental unit and any subsampling.
A table of treatment means with units, followed by SEm±, CD (5%), and CV (%).
The F-test results and the mean-comparison procedure used.
Any transformation, missing plots, and diagnostic findings.
An agronomic interpretation of the size of the differences, not only their significance.


report <- data.frame(Variety = names(sort(tapply(rb$yield_t_ha, rb$variety, mean),
                                          decreasing = TRUE)),
                     Yield_t_ha = round(sort(tapply(rb$yield_t_ha, rb$variety, mean),
                                             decreasing = TRUE), 2),
                     row.names = NULL)
stats <- design_stats(rb_fit, r = 4)
report

  Variety Yield_t_ha
1      V1       5.66
2      V3       5.18
3      V4       5.15
4      V2       4.99
5      V6       4.88
6      V5       4.48

cat(sprintf("SEm± = %.3f t/ha; CD (5%%) = %.2f t/ha; CV = %.1f%%\n",
            stats["SEm"], stats["CD"], stats["CV_percent"]))

SEm± = 0.098 t/ha; CD (5%) = 0.30 t/ha; CV = 3.9%


A suitable sentence would read: “Varieties differed significantly in grain yield (RCBD, four replications; F = 15.7 on 5 and 15 df, p < 0.001). V1 gave the highest yield (5.66 t/ha), exceeding the next best variety by 0.49 t/ha, more than the CD of 0.30 t/ha.” The numbers come from the analysis, and the chapter on reproducible reports shows how to insert them automatically.

13.14 Practical 14 and exercises

Generate and print a randomized field plan for an RCBD with seven treatments and three blocks. Record the seed.
Analyse crd.csv. Report the treatment means, SEm±, CD (5%), and CV. Which nitrogen levels do not differ significantly from N160?
Analyse rcbd_varieties.csv with and without blocks. Compare the error mean squares and calculate the relative efficiency. Explain the result in one sentence.
Draw the field plan stored in latin_square.csv and confirm that it is a Latin square. Why does the error have only 12 degrees of freedom?
In factorial_rcbd.csv, compare N0 and N120 within each variety using the appropriate CD. Explain why the main effect of nitrogen is not a sufficient summary.
Analyse split_plot.csv correctly and incorrectly. Identify every conclusion that changes and explain why.
Analyse aphid_counts.csv on the original and square-root scales. Compare the residual plots.

Chapter review. Replication estimates error, randomization makes comparisons fair, and local control reduces error. Each design is a way of randomizing treatments to units, and its analysis must reproduce that structure. Report means with SEm±, CD, and CV, choose comparison procedures in advance, and interpret differences in agronomic units.

13.15 Live R laboratory

Analyse a randomized block experiment
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
yield <- c(4.8, 5.4, 4.0, 5.5,
           4.6, 4.9, 4.1, 5.3,
           4.1, 5.0, 3.5, 5.1)
trial <- data.frame(
  block = factor(rep(1:3, each = 4)),
  variety = factor(rep(c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4"), times = 3)),
  yield = yield)
fit <- aov(yield ~ block + variety, data = trial)
summary(fit)
mse <- deviance(fit) / df.residual(fit)
r <- 3
c(SEm = sqrt(mse / r),
  CD_5pc = qt(0.975, df.residual(fit)) * sqrt(2 * mse / r),
  CV_pc = 100 * sqrt(mse) / mean(yield))
tapply(trial$yield, trial$variety, mean)
Investigate. Remove block + from the model and rerun. How do the error mean square and CD change? Explain why the blocked model is the correct one for this design.

Distinguish Pearson and Spearman correlation, interpret simple and multiple regression coefficients, check model assumptions and influential observations, and evaluate prediction on held-out observations.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.2 Association is not a treatment effect
text:
14.2 Association is not a treatment effect
Pearson’s correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between quantitative variables. Spearman’s correlation applies Pearson’s idea to ranks and describes monotonic association. Neither establishes causation, and a value near zero need not imply the absence of a nonlinear relationship. Both can be distorted by pooling unlike groups or by dependence among observations.
The simulated farm_yield.csv contains 100 independent teaching records with nitrogen application, seasonal rainfall, and yield. It is constructed for a regression lesson and is not evidence for a real fertilizer recommendation.

farm <- read.csv("data/farm_yield.csv")
plot(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha, farm, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Nitrogen (kg/ha)", ylab = "Yield (t/ha)")







cor.test(farm$nitrogen_kg_ha, farm$yield_t_ha, method = "pearson")


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  farm$nitrogen_kg_ha and farm$yield_t_ha
t = 11.9, df = 98, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.6741515 0.8385662
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.7687722 

cor.test(farm$nitrogen_kg_ha, farm$yield_t_ha, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  farm$nitrogen_kg_ha and farm$yield_t_ha
S = 40283, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.7582784 


Inspect scatter plots before interpreting a correlation coefficient. Pearson’s usual test assumes independent pairs and a suitable bivariate sampling model; ranks do not fix clustering or confounding. Spearman’s test uses an approximation here because rounded measurements can create ties.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.3 Simple linear regression
The model \(Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\epsilon_i\) describes a conditional mean response. The intercept is the predicted mean when \(X=0\); the slope is a change in mean response per unit increase in \(X\). Least squares minimizes squared residuals. The regression direction matters: a model predicting yield from nitrogen is not interchangeable with one predicting nitrogen from yield.

simple <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha, data = farm)
summary(simple)


Call:
lm(formula = yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha, data = farm)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.74926 -0.29294  0.02507  0.24883  0.95320 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    3.077606   0.135654   22.69   <2e-16 ***
nitrogen_kg_ha 0.018317   0.001539   11.90   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3957 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.591, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5868 
F-statistic: 141.6 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

confint(simple)

                    2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept)    2.80840521 3.34680622
nitrogen_kg_ha 0.01526255 0.02137163


The slope has units t/ha of yield per kg/ha of applied nitrogen. Its estimate is an association in these data, conditional on the specified model. If zero nitrogen lies outside the observed range, the intercept is an extrapolation and need not have a useful agronomic interpretation.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.4 Worked calculation: what least squares estimates
text:
14.4 Worked calculation: what least squares estimates
For a simple regression with an intercept, the estimated slope is
\[b_1=\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2},\qquad b_0=\bar{y}-b_1\bar{x}.\]
The slope is undefined when every predictor value is identical: the denominator is zero. A range of predictor values is necessary to estimate a relationship. The calculation below verifies the coefficients from lm() rather than treating its output as a black box.

x <- farm$nitrogen_kg_ha
y <- farm$yield_t_ha
b1 <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)
rbind(manual = c(intercept = b0, slope = b1), lm = unname(coef(simple)))

       intercept      slope
manual  3.077606 0.01831709
lm      3.077606 0.01831709


Residuals are observed minus fitted responses. With an intercept, least squares makes their sum approximately zero. This algebraic property does not show that their errors are independent or normally distributed. Those require design knowledge and diagnostics.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.5 Multiple regression and conditional coefficients

multiple <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + rainfall_mm, data = farm)
summary(multiple)


Call:
lm(formula = yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + rainfall_mm, data = farm)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.75803 -0.26042  0.02216  0.22680  0.66787 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    1.9792857  0.2317298   8.541 1.87e-13 ***
nitrogen_kg_ha 0.0179861  0.0013508  13.315  < 2e-16 ***
rainfall_mm    0.0017326  0.0003137   5.522 2.80e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3469 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6888,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6824 
F-statistic: 107.4 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

confint(multiple)

                     2.5 %      97.5 %
(Intercept)    1.519366311 2.439205177
nitrogen_kg_ha 0.015305102 0.020667040
rainfall_mm    0.001109939 0.002355324


The nitrogen coefficient now describes a change while rainfall is held fixed in the model. It may differ from the simple-regression coefficient because the models ask different questions. Omitted confounders, measurement error, and nonlinearity can still bias interpretation. Adding predictors raises ordinary \(R^2\) even if they contribute little; high \(R^2\) does not establish causality or reliable future prediction.
Strongly correlated predictors make separate coefficients unstable. In the crop trial, treatment and applied nitrogen are closely linked, so including both without thought can make individual effects hard to interpret. Select predictors using scientific reasoning, design, and an evaluation plan rather than repeated p-value searches.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.6 Residuals, leverage, and influence

old <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(multiple)







par(old)
head(sort(cooks.distance(multiple), decreasing = TRUE))

        52         81         74         10         94          3 
0.07415445 0.06520610 0.04821445 0.04345712 0.03896112 0.03604932 


The residual-versus-fitted plot checks mean structure, the Q–Q plot checks the error distribution, the scale-location plot checks spread, and leverage/influence diagnostics identify observations that can strongly affect estimates. Check influential records against source information; do not delete them merely to improve fit. Classical t-tests and intervals need assumptions about errors, including independence and constant variance. Normality concerns the errors for small-sample inference, not every predictor’s marginal distribution.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.7 Categorical predictors and reference levels
Regression can include categorical variables through indicator coding. A two-variety example illustrates this without requiring the varieties to be interpreted as numeric doses. The reference level determines the intercept’s meaning, while the fitted mean for each observation remains unchanged under a consistent recoding.

trial <- read.csv("data/crop_trial.csv")
trial$variety <- factor(trial$variety, levels = c("A", "B"))
trial$block <- factor(trial$block)
variety_model <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ block + treatment + variety, data = trial)
coef(variety_model)

     (Intercept)           block2           block3           block4 
       3.4150000        0.1941667        0.3391667        0.5725000 
          block5 treatmentControl treatmentMineral         varietyB 
       0.4166667       -0.7125000        0.5190000        0.2340000 


The varietyB coefficient compares B with A conditional on the other terms in this additive model. It assumes a common variety difference across treatments. The preceding ANOVA chapter explains how a treatment-by-variety interaction relaxes that assumption. ANOVA and regression are connected expressions of linear modelling, rather than unrelated procedures selected solely by the appearance of a response column.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.8 Residual standard error and explained variation
text:
14.8 Residual standard error and explained variation
The residual sum of squares measures unexplained squared deviations after fitting. Dividing by residual degrees of freedom and taking a square root gives the residual standard error, in yield units. \(R^2\) compares residual sum of squares with the total sum of squares around the observed mean:
\[R^2=1-\frac{\sum(y_i-\widehat{y}_i)^2}{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}.\]

rss <- sum(residuals(multiple)^2)
tss <- sum((farm$yield_t_ha - mean(farm$yield_t_ha))^2)
c(manual_R_squared = 1 - rss / tss,
  reported_R_squared = summary(multiple)$r.squared,
  residual_standard_error = sqrt(rss / df.residual(multiple)))

       manual_R_squared      reported_R_squared residual_standard_error 
              0.6888415               0.6888415               0.3469405 


An in-sample \(R^2\) describes fit to the observed response variation under that model. It is not the percentage probability that a prediction is correct. A narrow predictor range can produce a low \(R^2\) even when a small slope is estimated usefully; a common time trend can produce a high \(R^2\) for an unsuitable causal interpretation. Compare models in relation to their purpose and predictor domain.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.9 Nonlinearity and an apparent fertilizer optimum
text:
14.9 Nonlinearity and an apparent fertilizer optimum
Crop response to a nutrient may increase initially and then approach a plateau or decline. A straight line over a restricted range can approximate part of that response without defining a biological optimum. A quadratic model adds a squared predictor term. In R formulas, write I(x^2) so the power is interpreted arithmetically.

quadratic <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + I(nitrogen_kg_ha^2) + rainfall_mm,
                 data = farm)
summary(quadratic)


Call:
lm(formula = yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + I(nitrogen_kg_ha^2) + 
    rainfall_mm, data = farm)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.76092 -0.25807  0.02466  0.22923  0.67272 

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)         2.034e+00  4.050e-01   5.021 2.37e-06 ***
nitrogen_kg_ha      1.660e-02  8.536e-03   1.945   0.0547 .  
I(nitrogen_kg_ha^2) 8.248e-06  5.019e-05   0.164   0.8698    
rainfall_mm         1.730e-03  3.158e-04   5.479 3.44e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3487 on 96 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6889,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6792 
F-statistic: 70.87 on 3 and 96 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


For a concave quadratic \(a+bN+cN^2\) with \(c<0\), its mathematical maximum occurs at \(-b/(2c)\). If c is positive, the stationary point is a minimum, not an optimum. Even a concave fitted curve may place its maximum outside the observed nitrogen range, where it is unsupported extrapolation. The supplied simulation is generated with a linear mean response, so a quadratic term should not be presented as discovering a true fertilizer optimum.
An economic optimum additionally depends on crop price, input cost, and an appropriate response function. A fitted yield curve alone cannot supply those missing quantities. A defensible recommendation also needs replicated evidence across relevant environments and an assessment of uncertainty. In this introductory course, use nonlinear patterns to motivate questions and model checks before offering recommendations.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.10 Predict and evaluate honestly

new_farm <- data.frame(nitrogen_kg_ha = 80, rainfall_mm = 650)
predict(multiple, new_farm, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 4.544382 4.474566 4.614198

predict(multiple, new_farm, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 4.544382 3.852271 5.236493

set.seed(531)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(farm)), size = 75)
train <- farm[train_id, ]
test <- farm[-train_id, ]
fit_train <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + rainfall_mm, data = train)
pred <- predict(fit_train, test)
baseline <- rep(mean(train$yield_t_ha), nrow(test))
data.frame(method = c("Regression", "Training mean"),
           RMSE = c(sqrt(mean((test$yield_t_ha - pred)^2)),
                    sqrt(mean((test$yield_t_ha - baseline)^2))),
           MAE = c(mean(abs(test$yield_t_ha - pred)),
                   mean(abs(test$yield_t_ha - baseline))))

         method      RMSE       MAE
1    Regression 0.3892038 0.3225455
2 Training mean 0.6895416 0.5703840


A confidence interval concerns the mean response at the specified predictors; a prediction interval includes variation in a new observation and is wider. Both rely on the model. Avoid extrapolation outside the training range and consider combinations of predictors that may be unusual even when each is individually within range.
A random holdout is suitable for these independent simulated records. For repeated farms, spatial clusters, or time series, split by group, location, or time as appropriate. Fit preprocessing steps using training data only. One split gives an unstable estimate, so cross-validation may be needed for serious model comparison. The test set should not become another training set through repeated tuning.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.11 Practical 15 and exercises

Compare Pearson and Spearman coefficients and explain their target relationships.
Interpret the rainfall coefficient and its units. Why is it not automatically a causal rainfall effect?
Compare simple and multiple nitrogen slopes. Explain what changes in their interpretation.
Compare a confidence and prediction interval for the same new record.
Evaluate the held-out model against the training-mean baseline. Identify a realistic setting where a random row split would be inappropriate.

Chapter review. Correlation describes association; regression specifies a conditional response; prediction requires separate evaluation. Design and domain knowledge remain necessary for causal interpretation.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.12 Live R laboratory

Fit and interpret a yield model
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
trial <- data.frame(nitrogen = c(0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100),
                    yield = c(2.0, 2.6, 3.0, 3.7, 3.9, 4.5))
model <- lm(yield ~ nitrogen, data = trial)
summary(model)
predict(model, newdata = data.frame(nitrogen = 50), interval = "prediction")
plot(yield ~ nitrogen, trial, pch = 19, col = "#237f83",
     xlab = "Nitrogen (kg/ha)", ylab = "Simulated yield (t/ha)")
abline(model, col = "#bc7c21", lwd = 2)
Investigate. Interpret the slope with units and distinguish a prediction interval for a new observation from a confidence interval for the mean. Do not extrapolate this simulated linear response to arbitrary doses.







From the browser to your practical notebook



Record the input you changed, the output you obtained, and your interpretation. These live examples use base R and work independently. The full chapter examples, including package-based analyses, remain available with copy buttons for RStudio. Browser objects last until this page is reloaded; Reset code restores the editor text. Internet access is needed on first use; long or interactive desktop tasks belong in RStudio.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.1 Learning outcomes
Combine explanation with executable analysis, distinguish .Rmd from .qmd, add tables and figures, render HTML/PDF/Word reports, and share a project that runs in a fresh session.
crumbs: Module 7 · Reproducible research and AI-assisted coding
15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
section: 15.2 A report is an argument supported by evidence
text:
15.2 A report is an argument supported by evidence
A useful report states a question, describes data and design, explains decisions, presents results, and discusses limitations. Embedding R code keeps numerical evidence connected to its computation. If a dataset changes, re-rendering updates the results. This reduces transcription errors but cannot correct an unsuitable analysis.
R Markdown usually uses .Rmd source files and rmarkdown::render(). Quarto uses .qmd source files and the quarto render command. Both can execute R through knitr. Their configuration differs: R Markdown uses output: whereas Quarto uses format:. Simply renaming an old bookdown file is not a complete migration; chapter configuration, references, chunk options, and dependencies need checking.
crumbs: Module 7 · Reproducible research and AI-assisted coding
15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.3 Anatomy of a Quarto document
The following is a complete small document. The YAML header defines metadata and formats, ordinary Markdown supplies prose, and the R chunk computes a table. Save it as report.qmd in the project folder. The separate practicals/report.qmd provides a fuller working example.
---
title: "Plant growth: a reproducible analysis"
author: "Student name"
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
  docx: default
---

# Question

How do dry-weight measurements vary among the documented groups?

::: {#tbl-weight .cell tbl-cap='Mean dry weight by group in PlantGrowth.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
tab <- aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, mean)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|group | weight|
|:-----|------:|
|ctrl  |   5.03|
|trt1  |   4.66|
|trt2  |   5.53|


:::
:::

Interpret the estimates in @tbl-weight using the dataset documentation.
Use descriptive chunk labels; figure labels begin with fig- and table labels with tbl- for cross-references. A figure chunk can use #| fig-cap: "...". A hidden setup chunk may set #| include: false, but keep the source available to readers. echo: false hides code, not results. eval: false displays an example without executing it. Avoid hiding warnings until they have been investigated.

15.4 Dynamic values, figures, and interactive output
Inline R inserts a computed value into a sentence. For example, write the literal source 30 to report the number of observations. This keeps prose synchronized with the data. Do not hard-code a p-value in the discussion while the model updates elsewhere.
Use knitr::kable() for simple portable tables and ordinary R plots for graphics. HTML widgets such as Plotly need an HTML output context. In multi-format documents, test knitr::is_html_output() and use a static plot for PDF and Word, as demonstrated in the visualization chapter.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.6 Render and share
Run shell commands in the Terminal, not in the R Console:
quarto preview
quarto render --to html
quarto render --to docx
quarto render --to pdf
quarto render practicals/report.qmd --to html
PDF output requires a working LaTeX distribution, for example TinyTeX installed through quarto install tinytex. Install it only if PDF is needed. HTML is the default classroom format in the README instructions. Rendering the entire book to Word or PDF combines chapters into a single document. Opening an HTML file locally is not the same as publishing it to a public server.
Before sharing, restart R and render from source. Include source files, permitted data, metadata, package requirements, and instructions. sessionInfo() records R and loaded package versions. For a stable course release, consider a reviewed renv lockfile; do not claim that a package list alone pins an environment.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.7 Building the report in stages
Let us develop a report in the same order as an analysis. First create the document with its question, data source, and design, even before the final model is chosen. Then add a data-check section, followed by descriptive tables and figures. Only after examining those results should the methods and model sections be completed. This sequence makes the scientific argument visible rather than hiding it behind a final table of p-values.
An effective data section identifies the observational unit, sample size, variable units, collection period, and treatment or sampling scheme. State how the raw file was obtained and whether permission is needed to share it. In the cleaning section, explain missingness, corrections, and exclusions with their consequences for the analysis. Avoid including personal or confidential identifiers merely because they happen to be in the original spreadsheet.
The methods section should name the response, predictors or factors, model, and assumptions in terms that match the actual code. If the text describes a paired test but the code fits an unpaired test, a successful render has reproduced an inconsistency. Read both parts together. The results section should lead with the size and direction of important effects, followed by uncertainty and evidence. Keep mechanistic explanations and generalization limits in the discussion.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.8 Managing code chunks and dependencies
Each document is easiest to understand when it can be executed from top to bottom in a new session. The first chunk loads packages and reads inputs. Later chunks depend on those named objects. Avoid loading data by hand into the Environment pane and then assuming they will be available during rendering.


::: {#tbl-treatment-means .cell tbl-cap='Mean simulated grain yield by management treatment.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
means <- trial |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_t_ha), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(means, digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|treatment |  n| mean_yield|
|:---------|--:|----------:|
|Compost   | 20|       3.84|
|Control   | 20|       3.12|
|Mineral   | 20|       4.36|


:::
:::
The setup chunk is hidden in the displayed report but remains in the source. It does not install packages. The table chunk visibly records the summary operation. A future reader can distinguish a count of plot records from an estimate of mean yield and can rerun both.
Caching and freezing can save time in large projects, but they can also leave stale output when dependencies are misunderstood. During textbook revision, this project uses freeze: false so examples are executed again. Do not use old cached results to claim that revised code has been checked. For serious projects, record the environment and consider a lockfile, while recognizing that external data sources can change independently of package versions.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.9 Tables, figures, and numerical precision
A table title should say what was measured, how observations were grouped, and what the numbers represent. Put units in column headings where possible. Report enough digits for interpretation without suggesting unrealistic measurement precision. A yield measured to 0.01 t/ha should not normally be presented to eight decimal places merely because R printed them.
A figure caption should allow the graph to be understood away from the surrounding paragraph. Distinguish observed points from fitted lines, and describe error bars or shaded intervals precisely. “Error bars” is insufficient: are they SD, SE, confidence intervals, or prediction intervals? If an interactive figure permits hovering, retain axis labels and a caption so the static version remains meaningful.
Cross-references are preferable to manually typed numbers. After inserting a new table, @tbl-treatment-means updates its reference automatically. Manually writing “Table 3” can become wrong after reorganization. The same applies to chapter references and figure references. The final review should include checking that a referenced object actually supports the claim made in the sentence.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
section: 15.10 Reproducibility is also a classroom assessment
text:
15.10 Reproducibility is also a classroom assessment
Ask a classmate to open a copy of the complete project, restart R, and render the report. If it fails, identify whether the missing component is a file, package, path, or undocumented manual step. Record the correction in the project instead of asking the classmate to imitate your Console history.
Finally, read the rendered document as a reader. Are headings in a logical order? Do tables fit? Are captions readable? Do the conclusions match the estimates? A report can be computationally reproducible and scientifically weak, or scientifically thoughtful but computationally incomplete. Undergraduate training should develop both skills together.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.13 Live R laboratory

Generate a reproducible result sentence
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
yield <- c(3.2, 3.8, 4.0, 3.5, 4.6, 3.9)
result <- data.frame(n = length(yield), mean = mean(yield), SD = sd(yield))
result
cat(sprintf("Across %d simulated plots, mean yield was %.2f t/ha (SD %.2f).\n",
            result$n, result$mean, result$SD))
Investigate. Change a yield and rerun: both the table and sentence update. In a Quarto or R Markdown report, use an executable chunk for the table and inline R for values in the narrative. Rendering an entire report requires RStudio and Quarto.







From the browser to your practical notebook



Record the input you changed, the output you obtained, and your interpretation. These live examples use base R and work independently. The full chapter examples, including package-based analyses, remain available with copy buttons for RStudio. Browser objects last until this page is reloaded; Reset code restores the editor text. Internet access is needed on first use; long or interactive desktop tasks belong in RStudio.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.1 Learning outcomes
Describe what vibe coding is and where it fails for statistical work; write prompts that specify the question, data, design, and output; review AI-generated R code line by line; detect invented functions, wrong models, and silent data errors; verify results with known answers and independent checks; share a minimal reproducible example when debugging; and keep an honest record of AI assistance.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
section: 16.2 From an idea to a first draft
text:
16.2 From an idea to a first draft
Vibe coding is an informal term for developing software by describing what you want in ordinary language, asking an AI system to generate code, running it, and requesting changes. The term is often associated with accepting implementation details without examining them closely. For a statistical analysis, we need to go further: understand the code, verify the calculations, and justify the model. In this book, we use the conversational approach as an entry into reviewed AI-assisted programming. See the overview of the term.
For example, a student might begin with “Make a colourful graph of crop yields.” An AI assistant can draft a plot quickly, but that request omits the data structure, units, experimental unit, and purpose. A graph of treatment means, a distribution of individual plot yields, and a fitted response curve answer different questions. Clear agricultural reasoning makes a better prompt and a better analysis.
AI assistants are good at syntax, at remembering function names you have forgotten, and at explaining unfamiliar code. They are not responsible for your experiment. They do not know how your treatments were randomized, which plots were flooded, or why one value was recorded as -999, unless you tell them. Everything this book has taught about experimental units, missing values, and design-based analysis is exactly what you need to supervise an assistant.
crumbs: Module 7 · Reproducible research and AI-assisted coding

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.3 Using AI with R
One approach is to ask an AI chat assistant for a small R code draft, inspect it, and run it in RStudio. Another is to use an assistant integrated into an R development environment. Current examples include Posit Assistant in RStudio and Positron; their capabilities, access requirements, and settings are described in the RStudio guide and Positron documentation. Some editors can also show code completions from an assistant as you type. This lesson does not require a paid assistant or a particular model; tools change quickly, and the habits below apply to all of them.
Begin with a small task: explain a function, summarize a table, improve axis labels, or diagnose a reproducible error. Ask for the reason behind each change. Read unfamiliar functions in R’s help system and confirm that suggested packages and arguments exist. A plausible function name is not evidence that a function is available.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.4 The review loop
Productive AI-assisted programming follows a loop rather than a single request. Each pass is short enough that you can check it.



Table 16.1: The review loop for AI-assisted analysis










Step
What you do
What to look for




1. Describe
State the question, data, design, and output
Have you named the experimental unit and units of measurement?


2. Generate
Ask for one step of code with explanations
Is the step small enough to read in a minute?


3. Read
Read every line before running it
Do you know what each function does? Does it exist?


4. Run
Run in a fresh session on your data
Errors, warnings, row counts, and group sizes


5. Verify
Check one result independently
Hand calculation, known answer, or second method


6. Record
Save accepted code and notes in the project
Prompt, changes you made, and why






If you cannot explain a line, ask the assistant to explain it, then confirm the explanation with ?function_name. If you still cannot explain it, do not submit it.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
section: 16.5 Write a prompt that specifies the analysis
text:
16.5 Write a prompt that specifies the analysis






A model prompt for an agricultural practical



I am learning R. I have independent plot observations from a teaching experiment. The columns are treatment and yield_t_ha; yield is measured in tonnes per hectare. Use base R. Produce a table with total records, nonmissing yields, missing yields, mean, and standard deviation for each treatment. Keep missing values in the data and exclude them only from calculations that require observed yields. Do not replace missing values with zero, delete outliers, or run significance tests. Include a small simulated example, explain the code, and show how I can check the results manually.


Specify the question, experimental unit, column names and units, design, missing-value rule, and requested output. State restrictions such as “use base R” or “do not install packages.” Ask for one step at a time so you can inspect its result before proceeding. Share a small simulated example or a permitted, de-identified excerpt when explaining a problem; check your institution’s rules before sending research data to an external service.
A reusable template helps. Fill in the brackets and delete what does not apply.






Prompt template for an analysis step



Context. I am an undergraduate learning R for agricultural data analysis. I use RStudio with R [version].
Data. The data frame [name] has [n] rows; each row is one [experimental unit, e.g. plot]. Columns: [col] ([meaning, unit]), … The output of str([name]) is: [paste].
Design. [e.g. RCBD with 6 varieties in 4 blocks; treatments randomized within blocks.]
Task. [one step, e.g. fit the ANOVA model that matches this design and report SEm, CD at 5%, and CV.]
Constraints. Use [base R / named packages only]. Do not [delete rows, impute, change the design]. Explain each line in a comment.
Checks. Show me how to verify the result independently.


str() and dput(head(data)) are the most useful things to paste: they tell the assistant the exact column names and types without sending the whole dataset.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
section: 16.6 Worked example: review a generated summary
text:
16.6 Worked example: review a generated summary
The following is a teaching reference solution to the model prompt, not a transcript of a particular AI response. The simulated data contain a missing yield in the Control group. We deliberately count both rows and observed yields so the denominator is visible.

ai_trial <- data.frame(
  treatment = c("Control", "Control", "Control", "Compost", "Compost", "Compost"),
  yield_t_ha = c(3.0, 4.0, NA, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0)
)

summarize_yield <- function(x) {
  observed <- x[!is.na(x)]
  c(total = length(x), observed = length(observed),
    missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    mean = if (length(observed)) mean(observed) else NA_real_,
    SD = if (length(observed) > 1) sd(observed) else NA_real_)
}

ai_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(ai_trial$yield_t_ha, ai_trial$treatment), summarize_yield
))
ai_summary

        total observed missing mean        SD
Compost     3        3       0  4.5 0.5000000
Control     3        2       1  3.5 0.7071068

# Independent checks against calculations we can do by hand
stopifnot(ai_summary["Control", "total"] == 3,
          ai_summary["Control", "observed"] == 2,
          ai_summary["Control", "missing"] == 1,
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(ai_summary["Control", "mean"]), 3.5)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(ai_summary["Compost", "mean"]), 4.5)))

The Control mean is \((3+4)/2=3.5\) t/ha. Dividing by three, or replacing the missing observation with zero, would answer a different question. Its sample SD is approximately 0.707 t/ha; the Compost SD is 0.5 t/ha. With no observed yields, the mean is undefined; with only one observed yield, the sample SD is undefined. The function returns NA for those cases. Summary values alone do not demonstrate a treatment effect.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
section: 16.7 Worked example: code that runs but answers the wrong question
text:
16.7 Worked example: code that runs but answers the wrong question
The most dangerous AI errors are not the ones that stop with an error message. They are the ones that run. Suppose a student asks: “Write R code to do ANOVA on my variety trial in rcbd_varieties.csv.” A typical first draft looks like this:

rb <- read.csv("data/rcbd_varieties.csv")
draft <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + variety, data = rb)
summary(draft)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
block        1 1.3954  1.3954   34.21 1.93e-05 ***
variety      5 3.0359  0.6072   14.88 1.07e-05 ***
Residuals   17 0.6934  0.0408                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


It runs and gives a significant result. But read the ANOVA table: block has 1 degree of freedom. There are four blocks, so the block line should have 3. Because block was read as a number, R fitted it as a straight-line trend in block number, as in regression, rather than as four separate groups. The prompt never said that block was a grouping factor, and the assistant did not check.

str(rb)

'data.frame':   24 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ plot_id   : chr  "R01" "R02" "R03" "R04" ...
 $ block     : int  1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 ...
 $ variety   : chr  "V4" "V1" "V6" "V2" ...
 $ yield_t_ha: num  5.43 6.08 5.29 5.42 4.67 5.34 5.99 4.46 4.97 5.24 ...

rb$block <- factor(rb$block)
rb$variety <- factor(rb$variety)
fixed <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + variety, data = rb)
summary(fixed)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)    
block        3 1.5082  0.5027   12.99 0.00019 ***
variety      5 3.0359  0.6072   15.69 1.7e-05 ***
Residuals   15 0.5806  0.0387                    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Now block has 3 degrees of freedom and the error mean square is correct. A second common draft drops the block term altogether, aov(yield_t_ha ~ variety), which runs, but treats an RCBD as a CRD and inflates the error, as the experimental designs chapter showed. Neither mistake is a coding error; both are design errors. Checking the degrees of freedom against the design (blocks − 1, treatments − 1, and (blocks − 1)(treatments − 1) for error) catches both in seconds.

# A design check you can always run
anova(fixed)[, "Df"]

[1]  3  5 15

c(block = 4 - 1, variety = 6 - 1, error = (4 - 1) * (6 - 1))

  block variety   error 
      3       5      15

section: 16.8 Worked example: a function that does not exist
text:
16.8 Worked example: a function that does not exist
AI assistants sometimes suggest functions or arguments that sound right but do not exist, or that exist in a package you have not loaded. Before trusting a suggestion, ask R.

exists("aov")            # a real base R function

[1] TRUE

exists("anova_rcbd")     # a plausible but invented name

[1] FALSE

args(power.t.test)       # the arguments a function actually accepts

function (n = NULL, delta = NULL, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05, power = NULL, 
    type = c("two.sample", "one.sample", "paired"), alternative = c("two.sided", 
        "one.sided"), strict = FALSE, tol = .Machine$double.eps^0.25) 
NULL

"delta" %in% names(formals(power.t.test))

[1] TRUE

"effect_size" %in% names(formals(power.t.test))  # an invented argument

[1] FALSE


Use ?function_name to read the documentation, find("function_name") to see which attached package provides it, and packageVersion("package") to check the installed version. If an assistant says a function is in a package, install and load that package, then confirm with the help page. Do not keep asking the assistant to fix an error caused by a function that never existed; ask for an approach using functions you can verify.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.9 Verify with a known answer
The surest check is to run the code on data where you already know the answer. The previous chapters used a small example with groups A = (3, 4, 5), B = (4, 5, 6), and C = (5, 6, 7), for which the treatment sum of squares is 6, the error mean square is 1, and F is 3. Any ANOVA code, generated or written by hand, must reproduce those values.

toy <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 3)),
                  y = c(3, 4, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5, 6, 7))
toy_table <- anova(aov(y ~ group, data = toy))
toy_table

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: y
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
group      2      6       3       3  0.125
Residuals  6      6       1               

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(toy_table["group", "Sum Sq"], 6)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(toy_table["Residuals", "Mean Sq"], 1)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(toy_table["group", "F value"], 3)))

stopifnot() stops with an error if any statement is false, so a check like this can stay in your script and protect later edits. Other independent checks include comparing a mean with a hand calculation, comparing nrow() before and after a join, and comparing two methods that should agree, such as aov() with an Error() term and agricolae::sp.plot() for a split-plot.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
section: 16.10 Debug with a minimal reproducible example
text:
16.10 Debug with a minimal reproducible example
When code fails, the assistant needs the same information a human helper would: the exact error, the code that produced it, and a small example of the data. A minimal reproducible example (reprex) is the smallest piece of code that someone else can run to see the same problem.

small <- head(rb, 4)
dput(small)

structure(list(plot_id = c("R01", "R02", "R03", "R04"), block = structure(c(1L, 
1L, 1L, 1L), levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4"), class = "factor"), 
    variety = structure(c(4L, 1L, 6L, 2L), levels = c("V1", "V2", 
    "V3", "V4", "V5", "V6"), class = "factor"), yield_t_ha = c(5.43, 
    6.08, 5.29, 5.42)), row.names = c(NA, 4L), class = "data.frame")


dput() prints R code that recreates the data frame exactly, including column types. Paste that output, the failing line, and the full error message into your prompt. Ask the assistant to explain the cause before changing the code, and to change only the lines involved.
Useful follow-up prompts include:

“Explain why the number of observed yields differs from the number of records.”
“My error is object 'yield' not found. Here is names(ai_trial) and the failing line. Explain the mismatch and change only that line.”
“Review this model for a randomized block experiment. Explain how the block factor enters the formula before changing the code.”
“Check whether the degrees of freedom in this ANOVA table match a design with 6 treatments and 4 blocks.”
“Add units and a caption to this plot without changing the observations or fitted model.”

When a draft fails, provide the exact error and the smallest example that reproduces it. Avoid repeatedly asking an assistant to repair a long script without checking what it changes. A coding error and a statistical error are different: aov(yield ~ treatment) can execute successfully while omitting a block factor required by the design. A paired test, an independent-samples test, and a repeated-measures model are not interchangeable repairs.






Successful execution is only the first check



Inspect row counts, units, missingness, group sizes, model formulas, degrees of freedom, and assumptions. Verify at least one result independently. Check that plots and written conclusions match the computed output. Do not ask AI to keep changing an analysis until a p-value becomes significant. You remain responsible for the method and interpretation.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.12 Responsible use
Data privacy. Research data may belong to your institution, a farmer, or a funding agency. Do not paste confidential or identifiable data into an external AI service without permission. A simulated example with the same structure usually serves the purpose.
Academic integrity. Follow your course’s rules on AI assistance. Where it is permitted, acknowledge it. A short statement is enough, for example: “An AI assistant was used to draft the R code for data import and plotting. All code was reviewed, tested against hand calculations, and corrected by the author, who is responsible for the analysis.”
Honest reporting. AI may help draft a methods paragraph, but the paragraph must describe the analysis actually performed. Never invent citations, observations, or results to complete a report. Assistants sometimes produce references that look real but do not exist; check every reference in the original source.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.13 Save a reproducible record
Keep the accepted R code in the project and render the report in a fresh session. Record package versions, relevant prompts, substantive AI contributions, and the corrections you made. A simple log in your project folder is enough:

# ai-log.md (kept in the project folder)
# 2026-10-20  Prompt: RCBD ANOVA for rcbd_varieties.csv (template above)
#             Accepted: aov() model after converting block to factor
#             Corrected: draft fitted block as numeric (1 df); fixed with factor()
#             Verified: df = 3, 5, 15; CD checked by hand

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.14 Practical 17 and exercises

Give an assistant the model prompt above, or write your own proposed solution if no assistant is available. Compare its code with the reference calculation. Test an all-missing group and a group with one observed yield.
Ask an assistant for an ANOVA of factorial_rcbd.csv without describing the design. Then ask again using the prompt template. Compare the two answers and list the differences.
Find two functions suggested by an assistant that you have not used before. Confirm with exists(), ?, and find() that they exist, and explain their arguments.
Write a known-answer test with stopifnot() for a function that calculates CD at 5%.
Create a minimal reproducible example with dput() for an error you met in an earlier practical, and write the prompt you would send.
Write an acknowledgement statement for your integrated project.

Submit the prompts, reviewed code, verification results, and a short account of what you accepted or corrected. Explain every line you submit.
Chapter review. An AI assistant can draft R code quickly, but it cannot see your experiment. Specify the design in the prompt, read every line, check degrees of freedom and row counts, verify with known answers, and record what you changed. Code that runs is only the first check; responsibility for the analysis stays with you.

title: 16  Vibe coding: writing R with an AI assistant
text:
16.15 Live R laboratory

Spot the mistake in a generated analysis
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
# A "generated" analysis of an RCBD: 4 varieties in 3 blocks
trial <- data.frame(
  block = rep(1:3, each = 4),
  variety = rep(c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4"), times = 3),
  yield = c(4.8, 5.4, 4.0, 5.5, 4.6, 4.9, 4.1, 5.3, 4.1, 5.0, 3.5, 5.1))
fit <- aov(yield ~ block + variety, data = trial)
summary(fit)
# Expected degrees of freedom for this design
c(block = 3 - 1, variety = 4 - 1, error = (3 - 1) * (4 - 1))
Investigate. Compare the degrees of freedom in the ANOVA table with the expected values. Which term is wrong, and why? Fix the code with factor() and rerun. How does the error mean square change?







From the browser to your practical notebook



Record the input you changed, the output you obtained, and your interpretation. These live examples use base R and work independently. The full chapter examples, including package-based analyses, remain available with copy buttons for RStudio. Browser objects last until this page is reloaded; Reset code restores the editor text. Internet access is needed on first use; long or interactive desktop tasks belong in RStudio.

title: Appendix A — Datasets and measurement units
text:
A.1 Supplied teaching files
All CSV files use UTF-8 text, one header row, decimal points, and NA for missing values where applicable. scripts/generate-data.R deterministically regenerates the original simulations using seed 531; scripts/generate-design-data.py regenerates the experimental-design, transformation, and germination files (also seed 531). field_book_messy.csv was written by hand. They are educational constructions without a real geographical location or trial date.
block and replicate are labels, not continuous response measurements. The simulated soil nutrient names indicate quantity and units but omit extraction protocols; a real data dictionary must state the method, depth, date, laboratory, and quality controls.

title: Appendix A — Datasets and measurement units
section: A.2 Real datasets bundled with R
text:
A.2 Real datasets bundled with R
PlantGrowth contains 30 dry-weight observations in three groups. Orange contains 35 repeated measurements on five trees, with age in days and circumference in millimetres. iris contains floral measurements in centimetres for three iris species. Their official help pages are linked in the references. Consult those sources for original provenance rather than assigning a new location or treatment meaning.

title: Appendix A — Datasets and measurement units
section: A.3 Historical series retained from the original chapter
text:
A.3 Historical series retained from the original chapter
The time-series chapter retains its original four worked datasets, followed by the agricultural weather application. All examples execute from local files. The retrieval script is scripts/download-original-data.R; running it is optional because the CSV copies are already supplied.



File
Observations
Meaning and source




original-kings.csv
42
Ages at death, in years, of successive English kings beginning with William the Conqueror; original teaching series. The index is succession order, not a regularly spaced calendar year.


original-births.csv
168
Monthly New York City births, in thousands, January 1946–December 1959; original series.


original-souvenir.csv
84
Monthly Australian souvenir-shop sales, in Australian dollars, January 1987–December 1993; original series.


original-rain.csv
100
Annual London rainfall, in inches, 1813–1912; copied from the author’s supplied rain.csv, originally linked to the historical precipitation series.



These series are real historical teaching examples and are not agricultural simulations. Births and souvenir sales illustrate seasonal structure; the kings example illustrates smoothing of a sequence but should not be described as equally spaced annual observations. The original iris.csv is also preserved in data/, with the column capitalization used in the import lesson. The built-in iris object uses different capitalization and punctuation; inspect names() before selecting variables.
The project preserves the author’s unedited lecture notes, images, rainfall CSV, assessment scripts, and document files in source-notes/. Their substantive explanations and illustrations are now included in the reading chapters, with code repairs and additions. The separately authored time-series PDF in the original folder is not repackaged as original textbook content.

These solutions illustrate reasoning and provide runnable checks. They do not replace explanations in a student’s own words. Interpretations of simulated data apply only to the teaching exercise.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.3 Graphics, description, and EDA

soil <- read.csv("data/soil.csv")
x <- soil$available_n_mg_kg
c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x), variance = var(x), sd = sd(x), IQR = IQR(x))

    mean   median variance       sd      IQR 
37.56500 37.05000 58.55723  7.65227 10.62500 

table(soil$soil_class)


 Clay loam       Loam Sandy loam 
        20         20         20 


Nitrogen means, medians, SDs, and IQRs have units mg/kg; variance has units (mg/kg)². An extreme positive value generally shifts the mean and SD more than the median and IQR. More observations can improve precision of a mean without reducing biological variability among individual observations. Leaves from the same treated plant are subsamples unless treatment was independently assigned at the leaf level and the analysis supports that design.
An EDA memo should identify treatment–nitrogen confounding, variation among blocks, the simulated source, and the observational unit. Numerical summaries must be taken from executed output. A pooled nitrogen–yield trend cannot separate management components that vary together.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.4 Growth and time series

growth <- read.csv("data/growth.csv")
fit <- nls(biomass_g_m2 ~ A / (1 + exp(-k * (day - ti))), growth,
           start = list(A = 1000, k = .07, ti = 50))
predict(fit, data.frame(day = 75))

[1] 861.3136


Day 75 is inside the observed 10–120 day range, so this is interpolation. It estimates a mean curve response under the model, not an exact new quadrat measurement. The logistic inflection biomass is A/2; the Gompertz value is A/e. A fit based only on early observations may not identify the plateau reliably.
For forecasting, use the first eight years as training and the last two as holdout, as in Chapter 10. Report test MAE/RMSE for both methods. Fitting on all ten years first would let future information affect model selection and estimates. A centred moving average includes future values and is not a directly available real-time predictor.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.5 Inference, ANOVA, and regression

data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
fit_aov <- aov(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth)
df.residual(fit_aov)

[1] 27

TukeyHSD(fit_aov)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

$group
            diff        lwr       upr     p adj
trt1-ctrl -0.371 -1.0622161 0.3202161 0.3908711
trt2-ctrl  0.494 -0.1972161 1.1852161 0.1979960
trt2-trt1  0.865  0.1737839 1.5562161 0.0120064


The one-way global null is equality of the three population group means. There are 27 residual degrees of freedom. A Tukey interval excluding zero indicates evidence of a difference for that pair under the simultaneous procedure and its assumptions. A p-value of 0.08 is not proof of no effect; the effect estimate and interval show which magnitudes remain compatible with the data.
The paired soil test matches the same plots before and after. An unpaired analysis discards that pairing. The pest table has independent plot statuses as its units; expected counts must be inspected before trusting a chi-square approximation.
In regression, a rainfall coefficient is a conditional change in predicted mean yield per millimetre, holding nitrogen fixed. A prediction interval is wider than a confidence interval because it also represents individual-outcome variation. A random row split is inappropriate when observations from the same farm, future period, or nearby spatial cluster would leak information across training and test sets.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.6 Field experimental designs

rb <- read.csv("data/rcbd_varieties.csv")
rb$block <- factor(rb$block); rb$variety <- factor(rb$variety)
with_block <- anova(aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + variety, data = rb))
without_block <- anova(aov(yield_t_ha ~ variety, data = rb))
c(error_ms_rcbd = with_block["Residuals", "Mean Sq"],
  error_ms_ignoring_blocks = without_block["Residuals", "Mean Sq"])

           error_ms_rcbd error_ms_ignoring_blocks 
              0.03870556               0.11604444 


Ignoring blocks moves block variation into the error, so the error mean square rises from about 0.039 to 0.116 and the CD widens. The relative efficiency of about 2.6 says a CRD would need about 2.6 times as many replicates for the same precision. Blocks stay in the model in any case, because they were part of the randomization.
In the Latin square, error degrees of freedom are \((t-1)(t-2) = 4   imes 3 = 12\): from 24 total degrees of freedom, rows, columns, and treatments each use 4.
In the split-plot, the wrong one-error analysis tests irrigation against a pooled error that is too small for main plots and too large for subplots. Its irrigation F-value is inflated, and the irrigation-by-nitrogen interaction, significant with error (b), becomes non-significant. The correct conclusions are those from the analysis with Error(block / irrigation).

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
section: B.7 Tests for proportions and ratios
text:
B.7 Tests for proportions and ratios
For 212 of 250 seeds, prop.test(212, 250, p = 0.85) estimates 84.8% germination; the interval includes 85%, so the sample is consistent with the standard. For 152 purple and 48 white, chisq.test(c(152, 48), p = c(3, 1) / 4) gives expected counts 150 and 50 and a small chi-square statistic (about 0.11 on 1 df), consistent with a 3:1 ratio.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.8 AI-assisted analysis
A prompt without the design usually produces aov(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen * variety) with no block term, or with block left numeric (1 df instead of 3). Both run. The design check is the degrees of freedom: for 4 blocks, 3 nitrogen levels, and 2 varieties, expect 3, 2, 1, 2, and 15 for block, nitrogen, variety, interaction, and error. A known-answer test for a CD function can use the toy data with error mean square 1, \(r = 3\), and 6 error df: CD = qt(0.975, 6) * sqrt(2 / 3), about 2.00.

title: Appendix B — Selected exercise solutions
text:
B.9 Reporting and project evaluation
echo: false executes code but hides the code listing; eval: false does not execute it. A complete project includes data provenance, raw inputs, cleaning code, analysis source, environment information, and rendered output. Interpretive exercises should be marked for the connection between question, design, method, uncertainty, and limitations rather than agreement with a preferred p-value.

title: Appendix C — Glossary and R reference
text: C.1 Statistical language

title: Appendix C — Glossary and R reference
text:
Term
Meaning in this book




Population
The set of units about which a question is asked; define its crop, place, time, and management scope.


Sample
Observed units selected from a population. Convenience samples can limit generalization.


Experimental unit
Smallest unit independently assigned a treatment.


Observational unit
Unit on which a measurement is recorded; it may be a subsample of an experimental unit.


Replication
Independent repetition of treatment assignment at the experimental-unit level.


Randomization
A chance-based assignment procedure that helps separate treatment from nuisance influences.


Blocking
Grouping comparable experimental units before randomization to account for known variation.


Confounding
A situation where influences vary together so their separate contributions cannot be identified from the comparison.


Parameter
A quantity describing a population or a model, such as a mean or regression slope.


Estimate
A value calculated from data to represent a parameter.


Residual
Observed response minus its fitted model value.


Standard deviation
Spread among observations, in the measurement’s units.


Standard error
Estimated sampling variation of a statistic, such as an estimated mean.


Confidence interval
An interval constructed by a procedure with stated repeated-sampling coverage under assumptions.


Prediction interval
An interval for a new response, including individual-response variation under a model.


Effect size
Magnitude of a difference or association; its practical relevance depends on context and units.


p-value
Tail probability for a statistic under a specified null model and assumptions.


Interpolation
Prediction within the observed predictor domain.


Extrapolation
Prediction beyond the observed domain; it requires additional justification.


Holdout
Observations reserved from fitting for assessing prediction.


Reproducibility
Ability to regenerate an analysis from its inputs, code, and environment.

title: Appendix C — Glossary and R reference
text:
C.2 R language reminders








Task
Expression
Caution




Assign
yield <- 4.8
Names are case sensitive.


Compare equality
x == 5
= also occurs in function arguments; it is not an equality test.


Combine values
c(1, 2, 3)
Atomic vectors coerce to a common type.


Make a sequence
seq(0, 10, by = 2)
Choose spacing appropriate to units.


Select vector entries
x[c(1, 3)]
Indices begin at 1.


Select a table
dat[rows, columns]
The comma distinguishes rows from columns.


Extract a column
dat$yield_t_ha
Explicit names make provenance clearer.


Detect missingness
is.na(x)
Do not compare with x == NA.


Inspect
str(dat), summary(dat)
An import needs validation beyond these summaries.


Group and summarize
group_by(), summarise()
Summary rows represent a new observational level.


Fit a linear model
lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
Formula terms express a model, not causal proof.


Fit ANOVA
aov(y ~ treatment, data = dat)
The formula must represent the design.


Fit nonlinear growth
nls(y ~ formula, data = dat, start = ...)
Convergence alone is insufficient.


Inspect help
?function_name
Read arguments, returned values, assumptions, and examples.

title: Appendix C — Glossary and R reference
section: C.3 Common errors and a repair sequence
text:
C.3 Common errors and a repair sequence
When a command fails, read the first error, check spelling and object existence, inspect types and dimensions, and run the smallest relevant part. For file errors, check getwd() and file.exists(). For a missing package, check installation and loading. For a model failure, inspect the data and the model assumptions before changing optimizer settings. Keep a short note of the cause and resolution; debugging is a skill developed through explanation.

title: Appendix C — Glossary and R reference
section: C.4 Before you submit an analysis
text:
C.4 Before you submit an analysis
State the question and unit; document the source and units; retain raw data; record cleaning decisions; show distributions; justify the model; examine residuals; report effects and uncertainty; distinguish association from causation; and render from a fresh session. These steps are scientific habits, not a substitute for judgment.
